# Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value {#ch:FOUNDATIONS} The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. [Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system.]{.key-statement} The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know how its activity represents that value and what makes the activity variable. We begin with the spikes that cells send and the patterns of firing rates across a population. A model of spike counts then shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. We then learn how to tell whether measurements vary together and how to separate random spreading from a change in the average value. Those distinctions will let us interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion. ## Patterns of firing rates represent a value {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-SPIKES} [A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called [**spike**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} [A [**firing rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the expected number of spikes per unit time.]{.definition-explanation} A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. [Neurons affect one another through connections called [**synapse**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects: - [An [**excitatory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} increases a receiving neuron's tendency to fire.]{.definition-explanation} - [An [**inhibitory input**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} reduces it.]{.definition-explanation} The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. [When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has [**recurrent connectivity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears. [A [**tuning curve**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} gives a neuron's expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable.]{.definition-explanation} For eye angle $\theta$, a simple local model is $r_i(\theta)=b_i+k_i\theta$. Neuron $i$ has baseline rate $b_i$ in spikes per second and slope $k_i$ in spikes per second per degree. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.[^f-eye] Different cells have different tuning curves. The vector $$ \mathbf r(\theta)=\bigl(r_1(\theta),\ldots,r_N(\theta)\bigr) $$ [is a [**population code**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: the pattern across $N$ neurons carries information about $\theta$.]{.definition-explanation} The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. [Reading a value from observed spikes is [**decoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} [Establishing a population pattern from an input is [**encoding**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} [The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity.]{.key-statement} Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a place cell fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a place field. One neuron can have several fields. [A [**rate map**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there.]{.definition-explanation} Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model's expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.[^f-place] The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells, but their connections differ: - CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation. - CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation. [A [**grid cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena.]{.definition-explanation} These repeated grid fields and a place cell's irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1's output maps need not identify where the animal's position estimate is maintained.[^f-anatomy] ## A variable spike count at a fixed rate {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-POISSON} A tuning curve describes expected activity, but a brief spike observation can differ each time the same value is represented. [The 2012 model describes this variability with a [**Poisson process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. At constant rate $r$, the number $K$ of spikes in an interval of length $\Delta t$ obeys]{.definition-explanation} $$ \Pr(K=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}, \qquad \lambda=r\Delta t, \qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots . $$ Here $\lambda$ is an expected count, so it has no units. For this distribution, $$ \mathbb E[K]=\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\lambda. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: why a Poisson count has variance equal to its mean"} Summing $k\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda$. Likewise, summing $k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda^2$. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$, $$ \mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda. $$ ::: The count variance grows with rate, while its size relative to the mean falls. Its relative standard deviation is $\sqrt\lambda/\lambda=1/\sqrt\lambda$. This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.[^f-poisson]
[**Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population**]{#sec-foundations-count-example} Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is $20\times0.05=1$. The probability of seeing no spike is $e^{-1}=0.368$. A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive. Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation $\sqrt{20}=4.47$. The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. [Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If a common varying input makes several cells' firing rates rise and fall together, that shared variation will not disappear in the same way.]{.key-statement} The two count distributions can be compared on the same rate per cell scale.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-POISSON-POPULATION}}
Dividing the pooled rate estimate by 20 keeps the expected rate per cell fixed, while independent averaging reduces its relative spread. See [Poisson count likelihood, SI Eq. S43, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9).
For changing rates, the expected count is the integral $\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt$. In a recurrent network, $r(t)$ itself depends on past activity. The useful independence statement is therefore conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. Averaging over the evolving state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains. Two other measurements describe different aspects of variability: - [The [**coefficient of variation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, or CV, of interspike intervals, the times between successive spikes, is their standard deviation divided by their mean.]{.definition-explanation} A homogeneous Poisson process has exponential intervals and CV equal to one. More regular firing can have CV below one, as in the ocular motor neurons analyzed in 2022. - [The count variance divided by mean count is the [**Fano factor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}]{.definition-explanation}; its value also depends on the counting interval. CV and Fano factor cannot be substituted for one another without additional assumptions. ## Mean squared displacement combines random spread with mean motion {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-COVARIANCE} To identify where variability enters a pathway, the eye paper compares measurements that share some fluctuations and have other fluctuations of their own. [For random variables $X$ and $Y$, [**covariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} measures how their centered values vary together:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)= \mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])]. $$ It has units equal to the product of the units of $X$ and $Y$. Variance is the special case $\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)$. Expanding a centered sum or difference gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(X\pm Y)= \operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y) \pm2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y). $$ Independence makes the covariance zero when the relevant moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence in general. [The [**correlation coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} rescales covariance:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \rho_{XY}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)} {\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ It has no units and lies between $-1$ and $1$ for variables with nonzero variance. The magnitude of a correlation is not automatically the fraction of an output variance caused by a particular source. Establishing that interpretation requires a model of the signal, noise, and measurement gains. The [eye-drift covariance calculation](ch-eye-drift.html#sec-eye-chi) supplies that model for eye displacement. The quantity that changes between two times is a displacement $\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)$, where $\ell$ is a time lag. Its mean square splits into $$ \mathbb E[(\Delta x)^2]= \operatorname{Var}(\Delta x)+\mathbb E[\Delta x]^2. $$ [Thus a growing mean squared displacement can contain random spread, a systematic change in the mean, or both.]{.key-statement} [^f-eye]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., and Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Introduction, Figs. 1–2, and Methods, Eqs. 2–7. [^f-place]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., and Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017). Introduction, Results, and STAR Methods. The distinction between map randomness and visit-to-visit spike variation follows from what the model's random function indexes. [^f-anatomy]: Maimon, S. R., and colleagues (2026). *Sparse-to-dense coding transformation between hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1*. Nature. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10537-0). Main text, Introduction and Figs. 1–2. The present guide uses this later comparison for anatomical and coding context; it is not evidence reported in the 2025 paper. [^f-poisson]: Burak, Y., and Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(43), 17645–17650. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Results and Methods, Eqs. 7–10, describe the Poisson spike model and weak-fluctuation approximation. The finite count calculations in this section are direct consequences of the Poisson distribution and are guide derivations.

# Stable representations can accumulate error {#ch:PERSISTENCE} The next distinction is between a value and the activity that represents it. Eye position is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory] We first build a small example in which some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. We then ask what happens when small lasting changes arrive repeatedly, deriving how their spread grows with time and how a fixed bias changes that prediction. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. ## Stable activity with a vulnerable stored value {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR} [A circuit's current activities are its [**state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} A dynamical equation specifies how that state changes. [A [**fixed point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a state where the deterministic rate of change is zero.]{.definition-explanation} It is stable in a direction if a small disturbance in that direction decays. Memory of a continuous quantity calls for a family of persistent states. [A [**continuous attractor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and a neutral direction along it. Neutral means that there is no restoring force along that direction in the ideal deterministic model.]{.definition-explanation} [The family is an [**attractor manifold**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Its dimension counts independent coordinates represented on it, rather than neurons in the circuit.]{.definition-explanation} A line attractor has one represented coordinate; a ring can represent a periodic coordinate such as heading.[^f-memory]
[**Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle**]{#sec-foundations-attractor-example} Consider a teaching model with two activities $r_1,r_2$ in spikes per second. Let $b=40$ spikes per second and let $k=2$ spikes per second per degree. A stored angle $\theta$ corresponds to $$ r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta. $$ The fixed points lie on the line $r_1+r_2=2b$. Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as $$ x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b, \qquad \theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}. $$ Suppose each activity changes according to $$ \dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x, $$ where $a>0$ has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives $$ \dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0. $$ The first equation has solution $x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}$, so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state. At $\theta=5$ degrees, the rates are $(50,30)$. Compare two disturbances from this same state: - A disturbance of $(+3,+3)$ changes the rates to $(53,33)$. It creates $x=3$ but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to $(50,30)$. - A disturbance of $(+3,-3)$ gives $(53,27)$, with $x=0$ and angle $26/(2\times2)=6.5$ degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response. [In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle.]{.key-statement} The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow. {{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR}} This construction illustrates the geometry; it is not a fit to eye-neuron recordings. In a larger network, the direction that survives depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) derives the correct projection from the network's linearized dynamics.
## Independent steps with equal duration and variance give linear variance growth {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION} If persistent angular changes arrive repeatedly, their errors accumulate. Divide time into intervals of length $\Delta t$. Let $\xi_j$ be the change in the represented coordinate during interval $j$. The calculation assumes: - increments are independent; - each increment has mean zero; - each increment has variance $2D\Delta t$, where $D$ has units coordinate squared per time. After $n$ intervals, $$ \theta_n-\theta_0=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\xi_j, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\theta_n-\theta_0) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(\xi_j) =2Dn\Delta t. $$ Writing $t=n\Delta t$ gives linear variance growth $2Dt$. [To describe this limit with a continuous path, use [**Brownian motion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $W(t)$. It starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments with mean zero, and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}[W(t)-W(s)]=t-s$ for $t\geq s$.]{.definition-explanation} It describes the limit of many small, suitably independent fluctuations. A physical network need only approach this description over the time and noise scales relevant to the calculation. In this continuous diffusion approximation, $$ \theta(t)=\theta(0)+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \mathbb E[(\theta(t)-\theta(0))^2]=2Dt. $$ [The parameter $D$ is the diffusion coefficient. It measures the rate of variance growth; a single trajectory need not move monotonically away from its starting value.]{.key-statement} The mean squared displacement, or MSD, is the expected squared change across a lag. In the zero-mean diffusion just defined, MSD is $2Dt$. [A [**root mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is its square root, $\sqrt{2Dt}$, and has the same units as the represented coordinate.]{.definition-explanation} In several dimensions, adding independent coordinate contributions gives an overall MSD of $2dDt$ only when each of the $d$ coordinates has the same diffusion coefficient. A paper that defines its diffusion parameter as the entire two-dimensional MSD slope uses a different convention.
[**Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias**]{#sec-foundations-diffusion-example} Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. These are teaching values, not a new estimate from either monkey. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must therefore account for systematic drift separately. Sample paths show the irregular motion; exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A single path can turn back toward zero even while the root mean squared displacement grows. A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7).
Two times along a Brownian path are correlated even though its increments are independent. For $0\leq s\leq t$, write $W(t)=W(s)+[W(t)-W(s)]$. The bracketed increment is independent of $W(s)$ and has mean zero, giving $$ \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t)) =\operatorname{Var}(W(s))=s, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(W(s),W(t))=\min(s,t). $$ The same argument gives covariance $2D\min(s,t)$ for a diffusing coordinate started at a fixed value. This identity is the intermediate step needed to compute the error from averaging a memory that moves during readout. It also helps explain why smoothing a diffusive input is different from smoothing a stationary noise source. A finite range, a periodic coordinate, external feedback, or a position-dependent diffusion coefficient changes long-time behavior. For example, ordinary squared angular distance on a ring cannot keep growing linearly forever. The basic $2Dt$ result is local or unbounded unless those conditions are treated separately. ## A fixed spatial map differs from a value that wanders over time {#sec:FOUNDATIONS-RANDOMNESS} The memory and eye papers study fluctuations that accumulate as time passes. The place-field paper instead starts with a random function of physical position. Once drawn for a cell and an environment, that function is fixed while the animal moves through the map. Revisiting a place evaluates the same expected-rate function, although the actual spikes can still vary from visit to visit. These two kinds of randomness can occur together. A circuit may maintain a position estimate with time-dependent noise, while downstream cells respond to position through irregular but repeatable tuning curves. [Observing irregular spatial maps does not tell us how fast the maintained position drifts. Conversely, finding diffusion of a stored value does not determine the shapes of individual place fields.]{.key-statement} The following chapters develop the dynamical calculation first, then the experiment that tests a possible consequence, and finally the spatial statistics.[^f-place] The three questions can now be placed beside the kind of variation each paper studies.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-PAPER-MAP}}
The rows compare different questions; they do not establish a single circuit connecting all three papers. [^f-memory]: Burak, Y., and Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(43), 17645–17650. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Introduction, Fig. 1, and SI I–III. The two-activity example is a guide construction illustrating the geometry, not the paper's simulated network. [^f-place]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., and Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017). Introduction, Results, and STAR Methods. The distinction between map randomness and visit-to-visit spike variation follows from what the model's random function indexes.

# Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor {#ch:MEMORY-DYNAMICS} [A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value that the stimulus supplied.]{.key-statement} The important question is whether the activity pattern stays in the right place, not just whether activity continues. Burak and Fiete study this distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set.[^p1-model] To calculate the loss of accuracy, we first describe how spikes renew synaptic activity as it decays. We then follow a small disturbance through the circuit's return toward a stable pattern and identify the change in stored value that remains. Adding these lasting random changes gives a local rate of spreading. When connections have equal weights in both directions, we can express that rate using the cells' tuning curves and check its meaning in a two-cell example. The following chapter asks how this local prediction extends to longer delays. Paper and Supporting Information (SI) links open the cited PDF page, near the passage where the viewer supports it. Use the equation, figure, or paragraph label to find the passage; the PDFs have no numbered text lines. The memory coordinate is $\theta$. Its initial value is $\Theta$. A bar denotes a noise free steady state, so $\bar r_i(\theta)$ is neuron $i$'s steady firing rate at memory value $\theta$. The common synaptic time constant is $\tau$. A one dimensional diffusion coefficient $D$ has units of memory coordinate squared per time, with the convention $\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt$ when $D$ is constant and boundaries do not matter. ## Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity {#sec:MEMORY-SPIKES} **Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. [Incoming activations determine new firing rates; the resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.]{.key-statement} The model assumes fixed connection weights, constant biases, a common synaptic decay time, and independent Poisson spike counts conditional on the present rates. The connections are tuned to a continuous family of steady patterns. The Gaussian description below also assumes weak fluctuations in total input. **Mathematical derivation.** To combine discrete events with continuous decay, a count process records the events and a decay equation records how their effects fade. Here $N_i(t)$ counts neuron $i$'s spikes up to time $t$. The activation $s_i$ tracks the decaying synaptic effect of those outgoing spikes on receiving cells. It rises by one at each spike and otherwise decays: $$ ds_i=-\frac{s_i}{\tau}\,dt+dN_i(t). $$ Equivalently, if its spikes occur at times $t_i^\alpha$, $$ s_i(t)=\sum_{t_i^\alpha {{block:fig:MEMORY-SPIKE-TRACE}} The activation retains a decaying contribution from earlier spikes, so a spike train and its activation trace are different objects. The rate $r_i$ has units of spikes per second. The summed input and the firing rule are $$ g_i=\sum_j W_{ij}s_j+b_i, \qquad r_i=\phi(g_i). $$ The fixed weights $W_{ij}$ say how neuron $j$ affects neuron $i$, and $b_i$ is a constant input. [The [**neural transfer function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $\phi$ converts total input into a nonnegative firing rate.]{.definition-explanation} For example, increasing input might increase firing linearly over some input range, or exponentially. The paper allows general connectivity and transfer functions at first ([Model, Eqs. 7–9, p. 5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,372)).[^p1-model] Conditioned on the present rates, spike counts over a short interval $dt$ are independent Poisson variables. Thus $$ E[dN_i\mid r_i]=r_i\,dt, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(dN_i,dN_j\mid\mathbf r) =\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. $$ The symbol $\delta_{ij}$ is one when $i=j$ and zero otherwise. Splitting the count into its mean and fluctuation gives $$ ds_i=\left[-\frac{s_i}{\tau}+\phi(g_i)\right]dt+dM_i, \qquad E[dM_i]=0, \quad E[dM_i dM_j]=\delta_{ij}r_i\,dt. $$ This is still a jump process. [In the paper's [**weak fluctuation approximation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, many individually small spike contributions produce only small changes in each neuron's total input. Their summed fluctuation can then be represented by Gaussian noise with the same leading mean and covariance:]{.definition-explanation} $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt{r_i}\,dB_i, \qquad F_i(\mathbf s)=-s_i/\tau+\phi\!\left(\sum_jW_{ij}s_j+b_i\right), $$ where the $B_i$ are independent standard Brownian processes. The noise coefficient has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, so its product with $dB_i$ is a dimensionless activation increment. The Gaussian approximation is for small fluctuations in total input. It does not require each single neuron's entire spike train to look like a Gaussian process ([SI Eqs. S2–S5, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,128)).[^p1-weak] The supplement makes this limit concrete by replacing each population with $n$ equivalent neurons and dividing each connection weight by $n$. A summed input has a mean proportional to $n/n=1$, while its variance is proportional to $n/n^2=1/n$. Increasing population size therefore keeps the mean dynamics fixed and reduces input fluctuations. [For a ring network, a neuron's [**preferred angle**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is an angle where its tuning curve peaks.]{.definition-explanation} Increasing the density of equally spaced preferred angles and scaling weights as $1/N$ serves the same purpose. The paper's formulas give the leading terms in this large population limit, rather than exact finite network identities.[^p1-large] Setting noise to zero gives the deterministic rate dynamics $\dot{\mathbf s}=\mathbf F(\mathbf s)$. A continuous attractor is a family of fixed points satisfying $$ 0=-\frac{\bar s_i(\theta)}{\tau} +\phi[\bar g_i(\theta)], \qquad \bar s_i(\theta)=\tau\bar r_i(\theta). $$ **Interpretation.** In the noise free dynamics, recurrent firing balances synaptic decay at each fixed point. The network must be tuned to possess this family. An arbitrary recurrent network will generally have isolated fixed points rather than a whole line or ring of them. ## The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change {#sec:MEMORY-LINEARIZATION} **Neural mechanism.** A spike perturbs many aspects of a network's state. Most of those changes decay as the state returns to the attractor. [To calculate memory loss, we need the one change that survives: the displacement to a different fixed point. We assume a smooth continuous family with one neutral memory direction, while all other local modes decay. The disturbance must be small enough that the first order response describes the return flow.]{.key-statement} **Mathematical derivation.** [A [**linearization**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} keeps the terms proportional to a small perturbation and drops terms quadratic or higher in it.]{.definition-explanation} Here the network activation is $\mathbf s=\bar{\mathbf s}(\theta)+\delta\mathbf s$. Taylor expansion of the transfer function gives $$ \phi\!\left(\bar g_i+\sum_j W_{ij}\delta s_j\right) \simeq\phi(\bar g_i)+\phi'(\bar g_i)\sum_jW_{ij}\delta s_j. $$ The constant terms cancel because $\bar{\mathbf s}$ is a fixed point. # Spike information limits memory stability {#ch:MEMORY-INFORMATION} A neuron that receives spikes from a memory circuit can use them to estimate the value stored by that circuit. [Collecting more spikes helps distinguish nearby activity patterns, but during collection the pattern itself keeps moving.]{.key-statement} The same variability that limits readout also perturbs the recurrent network. Burak and Fiete connect these two effects by deriving a lower bound on memory diffusion from the information in the spikes.[^p1-info-main] The useful quantity is how clearly a short spike sample distinguishes nearby memory values. Comparing that quantity with the random motion already derived gives a minimum rate of memory spreading. This is a limit for a particular network, so using it to compare different networks also requires keeping track of what changes and what stays fixed. More information can permit better stability without ensuring that a particular circuit achieves it. We retain the memory coordinate $\theta$, initial value $\Theta$, firing rate $\bar r_i(\theta)$, synaptic time constant $\tau$, and diffusion convention $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D\Delta t$. The [network projection](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value. ## Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information {#sec:MEMORY-FI} **Neural mechanism.** Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction. In a short interval $h$, let $n_i$ be neuron $i$'s count. Treat the memory state as locally constant and use the conditionally independent Poisson approximation from the neural model. The calculation below uses positive rates. **Mathematical derivation.** [A [**likelihood**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability of observed data as a function of a proposed parameter value.]{.definition-explanation} For the neural model, $$ p(\mathbf n\mid\theta)=\prod_i \frac{[\bar r_i(\theta)h]^{n_i}e^{-\bar r_i(\theta)h}}{n_i!}. $$ Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum. With $r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$, $$ \ell(\theta)=\log p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =\sum_i\{n_i\log[\bar r_i(\theta)h]-\bar r_i(\theta)h-\log(n_i!)\}, $$ $$ S(\theta)=\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} =\sum_i\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i}(n_i-\bar r_i h). $$ [The [**score**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $S$ measures how the log likelihood changes when the proposed memory value changes.]{.definition-explanation} Its mean is zero because $E[n_i]=\bar r_i h$. Its mean square is $$ E[S^2] =\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i^2}\operatorname{Var}(n_i) =h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. $$ The cross terms vanish by conditional independence, and Poisson variance supplies $\operatorname{Var}(n_i)=\bar r_i h$. [[**Fisher information**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is this expected squared score. The paper divides it by observation duration and calls the result the [**internal Fisher information rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \boxed{J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}.} $$ [To understand why inverse information is an error scale, let $\hat\theta(\mathbf n)$ be an estimator whose mean equals $\theta$ locally. Such an estimator is [**unbiased**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Differentiate $E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta$ with respect to $\theta$. Under the usual conditions allowing differentiation through the sum over data, $$ 1=\sum_{\mathbf n}\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\partial_\theta p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =E[\hat\theta S] =E[(\hat\theta-\theta)S]. $$ The last equality uses $E[S]=0$. Cauchy Schwarz now gives $$ 1\le E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]E[S^2], \qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{Jh}.} $$ **Interpretation.** [This is the [**Cramér Rao bound**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It is a local bound for regular unbiased estimation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not guarantee that every finite spike sample admits an estimator attaining it. The paper works in a weak noise, informative sample regime where local likelihoods can be approximated as Gaussian and efficient estimation can approach the bound. [A [**prior distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the spikes.]{.definition-explanation} A strong prior, bias, boundaries, or globally ambiguous tuning changes the estimation problem.[^p1-cr] If the coordinate is an angle in radians, $J$ has units $\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The information in a locally stationary interval of duration $h$ is $Jh$, not $J$.[^p1-fi-source] A vanishing rate requires a suitable limit and regularity of the likelihood. Each cell contributes squared slope divided by its count variance per unit time. High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell's peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network's present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates. Two positive tuning curves with the same changing part isolate the effect of extra baseline firing.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-TUNING-INFORMATION}}
The rate peak has zero local slope, so it contributes no local information at that point. Extra spikes from a constant baseline increase Poisson variability without making nearby values easier to distinguish. See [Internal Fisher information, Eq. 3, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2). ## Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-BOUND} **Neural mechanism.** The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information. **Mathematical derivation.** Cauchy Schwarz bounds a dot product by the product of the two vector lengths. Here the normalization of the memory projection fixes that dot product, while the two lengths measure diffusion and information. From the [projection and diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), $$ 2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i, \qquad u_i=\tau r_i', \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=1. $$ Define two vectors $a_i=v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $b_i=r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Their dot product is $$ \sum_i a_i b_i=\sum_i v_i r_i'=\frac{1}{\tau}. $$ Their squared lengths are $\sum_i a_i^2=2D$ and $\sum_i b_i^2=J$. Cauchy Schwarz therefore gives $$ \left(\frac1\tau\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)=2DJ, $$ or $$ \boxed{D\ge\frac{1}{2\tau^2J}.} $$ **Interpretation.** This proof uses the general left vector formula, so symmetric weights are unnecessary. It is a shorter teaching reconstruction of the scalar proof in SI Section V. Its assumptions are those used to derive $D$ and $J$; it is not a general statement about all possible noisy memory systems.[^p1-bound-source] The units agree: $\tau^2J$ has units of time per coordinate squared, so its reciprocal has the units of diffusion. [Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it.]{.key-statement} **Neural mechanism.** [Reaching the bound requires the network's retained response to each cell's spike noise to match that cell's information about memory.]{.key-statement} A cell that adds retained noise without helping distinguish nearby values prevents equality. **Mathematical derivation.** Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional: $$ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. $$ Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, $v_i$ is proportional to $g_i'$, and $r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'$. At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of $\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)$. A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant $k$ throughout the relevant input range. Solving $$ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k $$ gives $\phi(g)=A e^{kg}$. **Interpretation.** This exponential family attains equality for symmetric weights with Poisson noise, under the other model assumptions. It is a sufficient condition, rather than a general necessity: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state.[^p1-equality] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule"} The [mutual-excitation example](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) supplies a counterexample to the unrestricted converse. Set its bias $b_0=0$ and use the linear rule $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ on positive inputs. Its fixed states are $s_1=s_2=\theta>0$, with $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Both rates are $\theta/\tau$, and both rate derivatives are $1/\tau$. Therefore $$ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. $$ Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio $\phi'/\phi=1/\theta$ changes between states. A converse that forces an exponential rule needs additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source's claimed converse, while leaving the information–diffusion inequality intact. :::
**Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.** In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At $\theta=0$ both rates are $1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and their slopes are $\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ per activation unit. Thus $$ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. $$ Here $J$ has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and $D$ has activation unit squared per second. The bound is $1/(2\tau^2J)=1000$, so equality holds at this balanced state. At $\theta=100$, the rates become $1500$ and $500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while their slopes stay $\pm5$. Now $$ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. $$ The actual diffusion remains $1000$. The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network's projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-BOUND-STRICTNESS}}
The gap at $\theta=100$ shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See [Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3).
**Neural mechanism.** When a circuit stores several coordinates, a spike can shift more than one of them. Comparing each coordinate separately would miss combinations of shifts. The information and diffusion must therefore describe these shared directions. **Mathematical derivation.** For $m$ memory coordinates the information is a matrix, $$ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. $$ The matrix calculation assumes that every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so $J$ is invertible. The matrix bound $2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}$ means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here $A\succeq B$ means $\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf z$. To derive it, form $N\times m$ matrices $U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Then $$ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound"} Set $Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}$. Expanding $Q^TQ$ and using $U^TV=I$ gives $$ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. $$ ::: **Interpretation.** The bound controls every combination of stored coordinates, including coupled directions that separate scalar bounds would miss. If $J$ is singular, this ordinary inverse formula cannot be used.[^p1-matrix] ## Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed {#sec:MEMORY-COMPARISONS} **Neural mechanism.** [The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed.]{.key-statement} Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input. **Mathematical derivation.** Increasing $N$ while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as $1/N$ keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as $N$ in the numerator and $N^2$ in the denominator. Consequently $D\propto1/N$, while $J\propto N$. This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor $a$, their slopes are also multiplied by $a$, so $J\mapsto aJ$. For equality achieving exponential networks, $D\mapsto D/a$ immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves $g_i'$ up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper's rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.[^p1-scaling] Changing $\tau$ while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives $D\propto\tau^{-2}$ in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because $\bar s=\tau\bar r$. In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as $1/\tau$, so $D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}$. **Interpretation.** These two statements concern different controlled comparisons. A larger cellular time constant can improve memory stability while the exponent of its effect depends on what the experiment keeps fixed. **Neural mechanism.** The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.[^p1-width] Assume preferred positions $\mathbf c$ have uniform density $\rho$ in a $d$ dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate $a$ and a common shape $f$: $$ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. $$ The width $w$ is varied while $a$, $\rho$, and the shape $f$ are fixed. **Mathematical derivation.** For one coordinate direction $\alpha$, replace the population sum by an integral and substitute $\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$: $$ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. $$ Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: - The volume element contributes $w^d$ because broader fields recruit more neurons. - The squared slope contributes $w^{-2}$ because broader curves change more slowly. Each diagonal entry therefore scales as $J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}$. Now restrict the tuning shape $f$ to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, $D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}$. **Interpretation.** The resulting comparisons are: - Narrower curves help in $d=1$. - Width has no leading effect in $d=2$. - Broader curves help in $d=3$. [These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes $a\propto w^{-d}$, giving $J\propto w^{-2}$ in every dimension.]{.key-statement} Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network's input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. The mathematical compatibility does not establish where a particular animal stores a memory, and the equality of tuning curves must be checked rather than inferred from the shared formula.[^p1-colocation] [^p1-info-main]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(43), 17645–17650, main pp. 2–4, Eqs. 3–5. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-fi-source]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 9–10, Section IV, Eqs. S42–S44; main Eq. 3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The score variance calculation is expanded for teaching. [^p1-cr]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, p. 3, Information-Diffusion Inequality and Saturation. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The scalar Cramér Rao proof is a teaching reconstruction of the bound invoked there. [^p1-bound-source]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 10–11, Eqs. S45–S49; main Eq. 4. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The residual matrix proof here is an equivalent teaching reconstruction. [^p1-scaling]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, p. 2, discussion after Eq. 2; pp. 5–6, Weak Fluctuations. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Comparisons with different held quantities are made explicit here. [^p1-width]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, p. 4, tuning width discussion. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The paper cites Zhang and Sejnowski's tuning work. The integral scaling and alternative firing budget here are teaching derivations, not a separate verification of that cited paper. [^p1-colocation]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. Such an estimator is [**unbiased**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Differentiate $E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta$ with respect to $\theta$. Under the usual conditions allowing differentiation through the sum over data, $$ 1=\sum_{\mathbf n}\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\partial_\theta p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =E[\hat\theta S] =E[(\hat\theta-\theta)S]. $$ The last equality uses $E[S]=0$. Cauchy Schwarz now gives $$ 1\le E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]E[S^2], \qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{Jh}.} $$ **Interpretation.** [This is the [**Cramér Rao bound**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It is a local bound for regular unbiased estimation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not guarantee that every finite spike sample admits an estimator attaining it. The paper works in a weak noise, informative sample regime where local likelihoods can be approximated as Gaussian and efficient estimation can approach the bound. [A [**prior distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the spikes.]{.definition-explanation} A strong prior, bias, boundaries, or globally ambiguous tuning changes the estimation problem.[^p1-cr] If the coordinate is an angle in radians, $J$ has units $\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The information in a locally stationary interval of duration $h$ is $Jh$, not $J$.[^p1-fi-source] A vanishing rate requires a suitable limit and regularity of the likelihood. Each cell contributes squared slope divided by its count variance per unit time. High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell's peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network's present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates. Two positive tuning curves with the same changing part isolate the effect of extra baseline firing.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-TUNING-INFORMATION}}
The rate peak has zero local slope, so it contributes no local information at that point. Extra spikes from a constant baseline increase Poisson variability without making nearby values easier to distinguish. See [Internal Fisher information, Eq. 3, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2). ## Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-BOUND} **Neural mechanism.** The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information. **Mathematical derivation.** Cauchy Schwarz bounds a dot product by the product of the two vector lengths. Here the normalization of the memory projection fixes that dot product, while the two lengths measure diffusion and information. From the [projection and diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), $$ 2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i, \qquad u_i=\tau r_i', \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=1. $$ Define two vectors $a_i=v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $b_i=r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Their dot product is $$ \sum_i a_i b_i=\sum_i v_i r_i'=\frac{1}{\tau}. $$ Their squared lengths are $\sum_i a_i^2=2D$ and $\sum_i b_i^2=J$. Cauchy Schwarz therefore gives $$ \left(\frac1\tau\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)=2DJ, $$ or $$ \boxed{D\ge\frac{1}{2\tau^2J}.} $$ **Interpretation.** This proof uses the general left vector formula, so symmetric weights are unnecessary. It is a shorter teaching reconstruction of the scalar proof in SI Section V. Its assumptions are those used to derive $D$ and $J$; it is not a general statement about all possible noisy memory systems.[^p1-bound-source] The units agree: $\tau^2J$ has units of time per coordinate squared, so its reciprocal has the units of diffusion. [Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it.]{.key-statement} **Neural mechanism.** [Reaching the bound requires the network's retained response to each cell's spike noise to match that cell's information about memory.]{.key-statement} A cell that adds retained noise without helping distinguish nearby values prevents equality. **Mathematical derivation.** Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional: $$ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. $$ Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, $v_i$ is proportional to $g_i'$, and $r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'$. At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of $\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)$. A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant $k$ throughout the relevant input range. Solving $$ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k $$ gives $\phi(g)=A e^{kg}$. **Interpretation.** This exponential family attains equality for symmetric weights with Poisson noise, under the other model assumptions. It is a sufficient condition, rather than a general necessity: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state.[^p1-equality] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule"} The [mutual-excitation example](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) supplies a counterexample to the unrestricted converse. Set its bias $b_0=0$ and use the linear rule $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ on positive inputs. Its fixed states are $s_1=s_2=\theta>0$, with $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Both rates are $\theta/\tau$, and both rate derivatives are $1/\tau$. Therefore $$ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. $$ Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio $\phi'/\phi=1/\theta$ changes between states. A converse that forces an exponential rule needs additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source's claimed converse, while leaving the information–diffusion inequality intact. :::
**Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.** In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At $\theta=0$ both rates are $1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and their slopes are $\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ per activation unit. Thus $$ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. $$ Here $J$ has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and $D$ has activation unit squared per second. The bound is $1/(2\tau^2J)=1000$, so equality holds at this balanced state. At $\theta=100$, the rates become $1500$ and $500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while their slopes stay $\pm5$. Now $$ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. $$ The actual diffusion remains $1000$. The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network's projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-BOUND-STRICTNESS}}
The gap at $\theta=100$ shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See [Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3).
**Neural mechanism.** When a circuit stores several coordinates, a spike can shift more than one of them. Comparing each coordinate separately would miss combinations of shifts. The information and diffusion must therefore describe these shared directions. **Mathematical derivation.** For $m$ memory coordinates the information is a matrix, $$ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. $$ The matrix calculation assumes that every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so $J$ is invertible. The matrix bound $2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}$ means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here $A\succeq B$ means $\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf z$. To derive it, form $N\times m$ matrices $U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Then $$ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound"} Set $Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}$. Expanding $Q^TQ$ and using $U^TV=I$ gives $$ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. $$ ::: **Interpretation.** The bound controls every combination of stored coordinates, including coupled directions that separate scalar bounds would miss. If $J$ is singular, this ordinary inverse formula cannot be used.[^p1-matrix] ## Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed {#sec:MEMORY-COMPARISONS} **Neural mechanism.** [The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed.]{.key-statement} Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input. **Mathematical derivation.** Increasing $N$ while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as $1/N$ keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as $N$ in the numerator and $N^2$ in the denominator. Consequently $D\propto1/N$, while $J\propto N$. This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor $a$, their slopes are also multiplied by $a$, so $J\mapsto aJ$. For equality achieving exponential networks, $D\mapsto D/a$ immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves $g_i'$ up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper's rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.[^p1-scaling] Changing $\tau$ while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives $D\propto\tau^{-2}$ in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because $\bar s=\tau\bar r$. In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as $1/\tau$, so $D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}$. **Interpretation.** These two statements concern different controlled comparisons. A larger cellular time constant can improve memory stability while the exponent of its effect depends on what the experiment keeps fixed. **Neural mechanism.** The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.[^p1-width] Assume preferred positions $\mathbf c$ have uniform density $\rho$ in a $d$ dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate $a$ and a common shape $f$: $$ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. $$ The width $w$ is varied while $a$, $\rho$, and the shape $f$ are fixed. **Mathematical derivation.** For one coordinate direction $\alpha$, replace the population sum by an integral and substitute $\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$: $$ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. $$ Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: - The volume element contributes $w^d$ because broader fields recruit more neurons. - The squared slope contributes $w^{-2}$ because broader curves change more slowly. Each diagonal entry therefore scales as $J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}$. Now restrict the tuning shape $f$ to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, $D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}$. **Interpretation.** The resulting comparisons are: - Narrower curves help in $d=1$. - Width has no leading effect in $d=2$. - Broader curves help in $d=3$. [These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes $a\propto w^{-d}$, giving $J\propto w^{-2}$ in every dimension.]{.key-statement} Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network's input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. The mathematical compatibility does not establish where a particular animal stores a memory, and the equality of tuning curves must be checked rather than inferred from the shared formula.[^p1-colocation] [^p1-info-main]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(43), 17645–17650, main pp. 2–4, Eqs. 3–5. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-fi-source]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 9–10, Section IV, Eqs. S42–S44; main Eq. 3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The score variance calculation is expanded for teaching. [^p1-cr]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, p. 3, Information-Diffusion Inequality and Saturation. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The scalar Cramér Rao proof is a teaching reconstruction of the bound invoked there. [^p1-bound-source]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 10–11, Eqs. S45–S49; main Eq. 4. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-equality]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 11, Eqs. S47–S51. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The linear-family counterexample is a guide calculation qualifying the source's converse. [^p1-matrix]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 10–12, Eqs. S44 and S52–S56. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The residual matrix proof here is an equivalent teaching reconstruction. [^p1-scaling]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, p. 2, discussion after Eq. 2; pp. 5–6, Weak Fluctuations. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Comparisons with different held quantities are made explicit here. [^p1-width]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, p. 4, tuning width discussion. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The paper cites Zhang and Sejnowski's tuning work. The integral scaling and alternative firing budget here are teaching derivations, not a separate verification of that cited paper. [^p1-colocation]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, pp. 4–5, sensory representation comparison and footnote concerning similarity of sensory and persistent tuning. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109).
