# Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed {#ch:MEMORY-READOUT} When a recall cue arrives, the stored value has already moved. Later spikes can help estimate the value present at that cue, but they cannot reveal the particular random displacements that occurred before it. Waiting for more spikes also allows the network to move further. [The question is how much observation helps when the value being read keeps changing.]{.key-statement} Separating the error accumulated during storage from the error of reading the cue state makes that question precise. Equal weighting of later observations shows why simply waiting can become harmful. Allowing for the state's motion then shows how observation can keep helping toward a limit, and how access to only some spikes changes the useful duration. The time constants and noise assumptions also need checking before the resulting limits can be compared with the paper's final error claim. As before, the memory coordinate is $\theta$, its initial value is $\Theta$, and its displacement variance is $2Dt$ for constant diffusion coefficient $D$ without boundaries or systematic drift. The storage delay $T$ ends at the recall cue; the observation interval $L$ begins there. The [spike information rate $J$](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures how clearly nearby present states can be distinguished, and $\tau$ is the basic model's common synaptic time constant. ## Storage loss and readout error add under specific assumptions {#sec:MEMORY-READOUT-SETUP} **Neural question and model.** At time $T$, a recall cue arrives. The observer now wants the original value $\Theta$, but only has access to future spikes. The network has already diffused during storage. Even perfect knowledge of the state $\theta(T)$ cannot recover its particular earlier random displacements. To solve the readout problem, the supplement approximates the likelihood from each short bin of duration $h$ as Gaussian. Let $x=\theta(T)$ and index subsequent bins by $k$. The equivalent observation model is $$ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k+\eta_k, \qquad y_k=\theta_k+\epsilon_k, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(\eta_k)=2Dh, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_k)=\frac1{Jh}. $$ The Gaussian increments and observation errors are independent in this approximation. The value $y_k$ summarizes information about the state from that bin's population spikes; it is not an additional directly measured physical coordinate. The continuous limit is a convenient mathematical description of the many spike, weak fluctuation regime. It does not assert that an arbitrarily short physical bin already contains enough spikes for a Gaussian fit. The derivations below are exact within this local Gaussian readout model.[^p1-read-gaussian] **Mathematical derivation.** For an unbounded coordinate with constant $D$ and no drift, let $x=\theta(T)$ and let $\widehat x$ estimate that state from later spikes. Write the storage displacement as $s=x-\Theta$ and the readout error as $e=\widehat x-x$. The total recall error is their sum: $$ \widehat x-\Theta=s+e,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(s+e)=\operatorname{Var}(s)+\operatorname{Var}(e) +2\operatorname{Cov}(s,e). $$ Assume the readout is locally unbiased at every possible $x$ and the future noise is independent of the storage history. Conditional on that history, the readout error then has mean zero. Since $s$ is fixed by the history, $\mathbb E[se]=\mathbb E[s\,\mathbb E(e\mid\text{storage history})]=0$. Both errors have zero mean, so their covariance vanishes. [In this readout model, [**translation invariance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that shifting the represented value does not change the statistics of the readout error.]{.definition-explanation} Its variance is therefore the same at every $x$; denote it by $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$. Using $\operatorname{Var}(s)=2DT$ gives $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L)=2DT+V_{\mathrm{read}}(L). $$ **Interpretation.** The two terms describe different sources of error: - $2DT$ comes from storage. - $V_{\mathrm{read}}(L)$ concerns estimation of $\theta(T)$ from spikes after $T$. The supplement derives this decomposition for a locally translation invariant diffusion and readout model; state dependence, boundaries, informative priors, or uncertain initial encoding require corresponding changes.[^p1-read-setup] A timeline separates the displacement accumulated before the cue from the error in estimating the cue state afterward.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-TIMELINE}}
Later spikes can improve the estimate of $x=\theta(T)$; they do not reveal the particular storage displacements that separated $x$ from $\Theta$. ## Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long {#sec:MEMORY-NAIVE} **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$. **Mathematical derivation.** Write $\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)$, where $B_D$ has Brownian covariance $$ E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s). $$ The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. The continuous average is $$ \hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt. $$ Count noise contributes $1/(JL)$: $n=L/h$ bins, each of variance $1/(Jh)$, give average variance $[n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)$. The motion contribution is $$ \frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds. $$ Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle $0\le s\le t\le L$, the minimum is $s$. Therefore $$ \int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds =2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds =\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}. $$ Combining the terms gives $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.} $$ The two contributions have opposite dependence on $L$. Differentiating, $$ \frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}. $$ At that duration the two error terms are equal, and $$ V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min} =\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** [Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.]{.key-statement}[^p1-naive] ## Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit {#sec:MEMORY-IDEAL} **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer; the readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval. **Mathematical derivation.** [The [**precision**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} of a scalar Gaussian estimate is the reciprocal of its variance.]{.definition-explanation} Independent Gaussian measurements of one value add precisions. To verify this, multiply likelihoods proportional to $\exp[-(x-a)^2/(2V_a)]$ and $\exp[-(x-b)^2/(2V_b)]$: the coefficient of $x^2/2$ becomes $1/V_a+1/V_b$. Let $P(L)$ be the precision about the state at the beginning of an interval of length $L$, using all observations in that interval and no informative prior. Suppose we have already compressed the later part into a likelihood about the next bin's state with variance $1/P$. Bringing that likelihood one step backward adds transition variance $q=2Dh$, since the next state equals the earlier state plus an independent Gaussian increment. Its precision about the earlier state is therefore $$ \frac{1}{1/P+q}=\frac{P}{1+2DhP}. $$ The new earliest observation adds precision $Jh$. Thus, up to bin endpoint conventions that disappear as $h\to0$, $$ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)}. $$ Expand the denominator for small $h$: $$ P(L+h)=P(L)+[J-2DP(L)^2]h+O(h^2). $$ The continuous equation and starting condition are $$ \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2, \qquad P(0)=0. $$ [The [**hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})$.]{.definition-explanation} [Its [**inverse hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} on $(-1,1)$ is $\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]$, whose derivative is $1/(1-z^2)$.]{.definition-explanation} Initially no observation means zero precision. The term $J$ adds new information; the term $2DP^2$ accounts for uncertainty when carrying that information backward through diffusion. Set $a=\sqrt{J/(2D)}$ and $k=\sqrt{2DJ}$. Separating variables gives $$ \int_0^{P/a}\frac{dz}{1-z^2}=kL, \qquad \operatorname{artanh}(P/a)=kL. $$ Taking the inverse function and then the reciprocal yields $$ P(L)=\sqrt{\frac{J}{2D}}\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L), $$ $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L) =\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L).} $$ [The [**hyperbolic cotangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\coth z=1/\tanh z$.]{.definition-explanation} This backward precision derivation is a teaching reconstruction equivalent to the Gaussian covariance calculation in SI Eqs. S58–S75. It makes explicit how diffusion limits the value of later observations.[^p1-ideal] For short intervals, $\coth z=1/z+z/3+O(z^3)$, so $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\frac1{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}+O(L^3). $$ The naive and ideal estimators therefore agree through the displayed terms. For long intervals, $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)\longrightarrow\sqrt{2D/J}, \qquad L^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2DJ}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The ideal observer keeps improving, but the improvement becomes small. Its variance relative to the limiting variance is: - $1.313$ at $L=L^*$. - $1.037$ at $2L^*$. - $1.005$ at $3L^*$. These are variances, so their ratios are not ratios of standard deviations. Using $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$ gives $$ L^*\le\tau, \qquad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt3L^*\le\sqrt3\tau. $$ [Thus the paper's statement about readout within a cellular time constant concerns a characteristic saturation time under full spike access. It does not mean all benefit ends abruptly at $\tau$.]{.key-statement} The naive observer's best variance is only $2/\sqrt3\simeq1.155$ times the ideal observer's asymptotic variance. Its best standard deviation is about $1.075$ times as large.[^p1-time] ## Limited access can make observation slower {#sec:MEMORY-PARTIAL} **Neural mechanism.** [A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.]{.key-statement} **Mathematical derivation.** If every spike is independently retained with probability $\alpha$, the observed rates and their slopes both scale by $\alpha$. Substitution in the Poisson information formula gives $$ J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_i\frac{(\alpha r_i')^2}{\alpha\bar r_i}=\alpha J. $$ The network diffusion coefficient stays $D$. Hence $$ L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2D\alpha J}} =\frac{L^*}{\sqrt\alpha}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{ideal,obs}}(\infty)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{\alpha J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The same factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$ multiplies the naive optimal interval and its minimum variance. The information bound implies $L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*\le\tau/\sqrt\alpha$, which can exceed $\tau$. A selected subset of neurons has exactly $\alpha J$ only when it carries that fraction of the information; a fraction of neurons or spikes chosen by a biased rule need not do so.[^p1-partial]
**Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval.** Take $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, $J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These values attain the information bound. Full access gives $L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and limiting readout variance $0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum is $0.1732\,\mathrm{s}$ with variance $0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. If $\alpha=0.1$, then $J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ideal characteristic interval becomes $0.3162\,\mathrm{s}$ and its limiting variance becomes $0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum becomes $0.5477\,\mathrm{s}$. A two second storage delay contributes $2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2$ in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances $0.021$ and $0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. Longer observation can reduce the readout cost; it cannot undo the random displacement during the delay.
## Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition {#sec:MEMORY-EXTENSIONS} **Neural mechanism.** The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters? In the basic model, the firing rate changes immediately when the summed input changes. Assume symmetric weights. The extension instead lets $r_i$ approach $\phi(g_i)$ gradually, with time constant $\tau_m$, while synaptic activation still decays with time constant $\tau$: $$ \dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i+\xi_i, \qquad \tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i). $$ Here $\xi_i$ is the zero mean noise from variable spike generation, with the same Poisson strength as in the basic model. **Mathematical derivation.** In this symmetric weight extension, the linear state is $(\delta\mathbf s,\delta\mathbf r)$ and its deterministic matrix is $$ A=\begin{pmatrix} -I/\tau&I\\ \operatorname{diag}(\phi')W/\tau_m&-I/\tau_m \end{pmatrix}. $$ The right tangent is $(\tau\mathbf r',\mathbf r')$. Write the left zero vector as $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$. The second block of $(\mathbf a^T,\mathbf b^T)A=0$ gives $\mathbf b=\tau_m\mathbf a$. The first then gives $W^T\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\mathbf a=\mathbf a/\tau$, so symmetry again permits $\mathbf a\propto\mathbf g'$. Normalizing its dot product with the right tangent yields $$ a_i=\frac{g_i'}{(\tau+\tau_m)\sum_jg_j'r_j'}. $$ Only the $s$ block receives the modeled spike noise, so $2D=\sum_i a_i^2\bar r_i$. The symmetric formula consequently becomes $$ 2D=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {(\tau+\tau_m)^2[\sum_i g_i'r_i']^2}, \qquad 2D\ge\frac{J^{-1}}{(\tau+\tau_m)^2}. $$ **Interpretation.** The sum of the two time constants replaces $\tau$. The larger one dominates when they are very different. This result belongs to the two stage model and noise placement just described; the paper does not prove that arbitrary collections of biological time constants can always be added.[^p1-two-times] **Neural question and model.** The equality condition also depends on the noise law. To see why, replace Poisson spike-count fluctuations with independent additive Gaussian noise of constant strength $q>0$: $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt q\,dB_i. $$ **Mathematical derivation.** The short interval observation of the mean rate is now Gaussian with variance $q/h$. Repeating the score calculation gives $J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/q$, while projection gives $2D=q\sum_i v_i^2$. The same Cauchy Schwarz proof yields $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$. Equality requires $v_i\propto r_i'$ because all cells have the same noise strength. In a symmetric network $v_i\propto g_i'$, so a linear transfer rule supplies the condition by keeping $\phi'(g)$ constant across participating inputs. **Interpretation.** In the Poisson case, variance grows with rate and an exponential rule is a sufficient way to attain equality. The pointwise projection condition remains the general criterion, including the [linear-family counterexample](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) already derived. The difference between these sufficient classes follows from the noise weighting, not from linearity being universally preferable.[^p1-gaussian] This explicit $q$ formulation is a teaching reconstruction that keeps dimensions and the noise normalization visible. The supplement's Gaussian subsection establishes the change in equality condition. Here the matched noise and likelihood derivation supplies all factors of $q$ and $\tau$ without requiring the reader to infer a normalization from SI Eqs. S94–S95. ## Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification {#sec:MEMORY-FIG3-AND-CAUTION} Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by $\sqrt{2D/J}$ and duration by $L^*$. In these axes the ideal curve is $\coth z$ and the naive curve is $z/3+1/z$. Both diverge like $1/z$ at short durations because too few spikes are available. The plotted features are: - The ideal solid curve approaches one. - The naive dashed curve reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$, then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states. - The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum. The storage delay contribution $2DT$ is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when $\alpha=0.1$.[^p1-fig3]
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-CURVES}}
More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved. One printed inequality deserves special care. Main Eq. 6 says that total error is at least $2D(T+\tau)$; SI Eq. S83 likewise uses a lower bound with readout term $2D\tau/\sqrt\alpha$. But the paper's other derived results imply $$ 2DJ\ge\tau^{-2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\ge\frac1{2D\tau^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\le2D\tau. $$ Thus the ideal asymptotic readout term is at most $2D\tau$, with equality when the information diffusion inequality is saturated. Substituting an upper bound for this term cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error. Within the local Gaussian model, the defensible statement is $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L) \ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}, $$ with equality approached as $L\to\infty$ for the ideal observer. At saturation this asymptotic expression becomes $2D(T+\tau)$. For partial access the same issue occurs with the factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$. This is an apparent inconsistency between printed formulas, identified by algebra using the supplied sources. It is not a claim that the authors issued a correction.[^p1-printed] For a concrete strict inequality case, keep $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$ but set $J=40{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Then $2DJ=400\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ exceeds $\tau^{-2}=100\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The limiting readout variance is $0.0005\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, whereas $2D\tau=0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. At $T=2\,\mathrm{s}$, the Gaussian ideal total limit is $0.0205\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, below $2D(T+\tau)=0.021\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. These values expose the algebraic problem without assuming the bound is saturated. When a continuous attractor circuit is used to accumulate an incoming signal over time, its stored value represents the integral of that signal. The short useful readout interval does not imply a short lifetime for this accumulated value. A tuned circuit can continue to represent the mean of accumulated inputs while its variance grows. A leak would instead pull its mean toward a particular value. [Diffusion limits the accuracy of the integral and the usefulness of long observation; it does not by itself introduce that restoring pull.]{.key-statement} Applying these predictions to an animal also requires checking its spike statistics, tuning, drift, access to spikes, and other sources of movement noise.[^p1-integrator] [^p1-read-setup]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-read-gaussian]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 13, Eqs. S58–S63 and the approximation paragraph preceding them. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-naive]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 15–16, Eqs. S76–S81. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The double integral calculation exposes the cross time covariance terms compressed in the printed derivation. [^p1-ideal]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 13–15, Eqs. S58–S75. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The supplement identifies the solution with a reverse Kalman filter. Here the equivalent precision recursion supplies a derivation without assuming prior knowledge of that filter. The printed plus sign in S71 does not match its hyperbolic cosine solution S73; the recursion independently gives the final S75 result. [^p1-time]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, main Eq. 5 and Optimal Observation Time; Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S80–S81. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-partial]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 16, Incomplete readout, Eq. S82 and Fig. S2. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The random thinning derivation states when the fraction of spikes equals the fraction of information. [^p1-two-times]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 17–18, Eqs. S84–S92. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The linear matrix here follows directly from S84; its rate decay block is negative, as required by that differential equation, despite the positive sign printed in the corresponding block of S85. [^p1-gaussian]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 19, White Gaussian noise, Eqs. S93–S95; main pp. 3–4. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Constant noise strength $q$ and its likelihood are retained explicitly in the guide's reconstruction. [^p1-fig3]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, Fig. 3, p. 4; Supporting Text, Fig. S2, p. 16. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The caption's readout equation numbers are stale relative to the supplied supplement; the corresponding results are S75 and S79–S81. [^p1-printed]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, main Eqs. 4–6; Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S83. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The inequality direction is checked algebraically here, without assuming an author correction or changing the supplied source. [^p1-integrator]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, Discussion, p. 5; Supporting Text, Integration time constant, p. 17. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109).

{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-TIMELINE}}
Later spikes can improve the estimate of $x=\theta(T)$; they do not reveal the particular storage displacements that separated $x$ from $\Theta$. ## Equal weighting becomes harmful when observation lasts too long {#sec:MEMORY-NAIVE} **Neural question and model.** A decoder designed for a stationary state averages its observations with equal weight. That reduces independent observation noise, but late observations reflect a state that has moved further from $x$. **Mathematical derivation.** Write $\theta(T+t)=x+B_D(t)$, where $B_D$ has Brownian covariance $$ E[B_D(t)B_D(s)]=2D\min(t,s). $$ The covariance arises because the two values share increments up to the earlier time. Their later increments are independent. The continuous average is $$ \hat x_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1L\int_0^L y(t)dt. $$ Count noise contributes $1/(JL)$: $n=L/h$ bins, each of variance $1/(Jh)$, give average variance $[n/(Jh)]/n^2=1/(JL)$. The motion contribution is $$ \frac{2D}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds. $$ Split the square into its two equal triangles. On the triangle $0\le s\le t\le L$, the minimum is $s$. Therefore $$ \int_0^L\int_0^L\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds =2\int_0^L\!dt\int_0^t\!s\,ds =\int_0^L t^2dt=\frac{L^3}{3}. $$ Combining the terms gives $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{naive}}(L)=\frac{2DL}{3}+\frac1{JL}.} $$ The two contributions have opposite dependence on $L$. Differentiating, $$ \frac{dV_{\mathrm{naive}}}{dL}=\frac{2D}{3}-\frac1{JL^2}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt{\frac3{2DJ}}. $$ At that duration the two error terms are equal, and $$ V_{\mathrm{naive}}^{\min} =\frac2{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** [Waiting longer eventually increases error, even with more spikes available. The problem is their equal weighting for a moving state.]{.key-statement}[^p1-naive] ## Accounting for diffusion makes readout improve toward a limit {#sec:MEMORY-IDEAL} **Neural question and model.** An observer that accounts for diffusion can use later observations without confusing them with direct measurements of $x$. Their value is limited by the motion separating them from $x$. This is an ideal inference rule for an observer; the readout calculation does not demonstrate a neural circuit implementing it. Its error can be derived by combining information backward from the end of the observation interval. **Mathematical derivation.** [The [**precision**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} of a scalar Gaussian estimate is the reciprocal of its variance.]{.definition-explanation} Independent Gaussian measurements of one value add precisions. To verify this, multiply likelihoods proportional to $\exp[-(x-a)^2/(2V_a)]$ and $\exp[-(x-b)^2/(2V_b)]$: the coefficient of $x^2/2$ becomes $1/V_a+1/V_b$. Let $P(L)$ be the precision about the state at the beginning of an interval of length $L$, using all observations in that interval and no informative prior. Suppose we have already compressed the later part into a likelihood about the next bin's state with variance $1/P$. Bringing that likelihood one step backward adds transition variance $q=2Dh$, since the next state equals the earlier state plus an independent Gaussian increment. Its precision about the earlier state is therefore $$ \frac{1}{1/P+q}=\frac{P}{1+2DhP}. $$ The new earliest observation adds precision $Jh$. Thus, up to bin endpoint conventions that disappear as $h\to0$, $$ P(L+h)=Jh+\frac{P(L)}{1+2DhP(L)}. $$ Expand the denominator for small $h$: $$ P(L+h)=P(L)+[J-2DP(L)^2]h+O(h^2). $$ The continuous equation and starting condition are $$ \frac{dP}{dL}=J-2DP^2, \qquad P(0)=0. $$ [The [**hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})$.]{.definition-explanation} [Its [**inverse hyperbolic tangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} on $(-1,1)$ is $\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]$, whose derivative is $1/(1-z^2)$.]{.definition-explanation} Initially no observation means zero precision. The term $J$ adds new information; the term $2DP^2$ accounts for uncertainty when carrying that information backward through diffusion. Set $a=\sqrt{J/(2D)}$ and $k=\sqrt{2DJ}$. Separating variables gives $$ \int_0^{P/a}\frac{dz}{1-z^2}=kL, \qquad \operatorname{artanh}(P/a)=kL. $$ Taking the inverse function and then the reciprocal yields $$ P(L)=\sqrt{\frac{J}{2D}}\tanh(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L), $$ $$ \boxed{V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L) =\sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\coth(\sqrt{2DJ}\,L).} $$ [The [**hyperbolic cotangent**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $\coth z=1/\tanh z$.]{.definition-explanation} This backward precision derivation is a teaching reconstruction equivalent to the Gaussian covariance calculation in SI Eqs. S58–S75. It makes explicit how diffusion limits the value of later observations.[^p1-ideal] For short intervals, $\coth z=1/z+z/3+O(z^3)$, so $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)=\frac1{JL}+\frac{2DL}{3}+O(L^3). $$ The naive and ideal estimators therefore agree through the displayed terms. For long intervals, $$ V_{\mathrm{ideal}}(L)\longrightarrow\sqrt{2D/J}, \qquad L^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2DJ}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The ideal observer keeps improving, but the improvement becomes small. Its variance relative to the limiting variance is: - $1.313$ at $L=L^*$. - $1.037$ at $2L^*$. - $1.005$ at $3L^*$. These are variances, so their ratios are not ratios of standard deviations. Using $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$ gives $$ L^*\le\tau, \qquad L_{\mathrm{naive}}^*=\sqrt3L^*\le\sqrt3\tau. $$ [Thus the paper's statement about readout within a cellular time constant concerns a characteristic saturation time under full spike access. It does not mean all benefit ends abruptly at $\tau$.]{.key-statement} The naive observer's best variance is only $2/\sqrt3\simeq1.155$ times the ideal observer's asymptotic variance. Its best standard deviation is about $1.075$ times as large.[^p1-time] ## Limited access can make observation slower {#sec:MEMORY-PARTIAL} **Neural mechanism.** [A downstream area may receive only some of the memory network's spikes. That reduces its information without reducing the fluctuations that already move the full memory network.]{.key-statement} **Mathematical derivation.** If every spike is independently retained with probability $\alpha$, the observed rates and their slopes both scale by $\alpha$. Substitution in the Poisson information formula gives $$ J_{\mathrm{obs}}=\sum_i\frac{(\alpha r_i')^2}{\alpha\bar r_i}=\alpha J. $$ The network diffusion coefficient stays $D$. Hence $$ L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*=\frac1{\sqrt{2D\alpha J}} =\frac{L^*}{\sqrt\alpha}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{ideal,obs}}(\infty)=\sqrt{\frac{2D}{\alpha J}}. $$ **Interpretation.** The same factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$ multiplies the naive optimal interval and its minimum variance. The information bound implies $L_{\mathrm{obs}}^*\le\tau/\sqrt\alpha$, which can exceed $\tau$. A selected subset of neurons has exactly $\alpha J$ only when it carries that fraction of the information; a fraction of neurons or spikes chosen by a biased rule need not do so.[^p1-partial]
**Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval.** Take $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, $J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These values attain the information bound. Full access gives $L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and limiting readout variance $0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum is $0.1732\,\mathrm{s}$ with variance $0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. If $\alpha=0.1$, then $J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ideal characteristic interval becomes $0.3162\,\mathrm{s}$ and its limiting variance becomes $0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum becomes $0.5477\,\mathrm{s}$. A two second storage delay contributes $2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2$ in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances $0.021$ and $0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. Longer observation can reduce the readout cost; it cannot undo the random displacement during the delay.
## Time scales and noise laws change the bound and its equality condition {#sec:MEMORY-EXTENSIONS} **Neural mechanism.** The time constant in the inequality comes from the dynamics that carry an activation fluctuation into a lasting memory change. If both synaptic activation and firing rate adjust gradually, which time constant matters? In the basic model, the firing rate changes immediately when the summed input changes. Assume symmetric weights. The extension instead lets $r_i$ approach $\phi(g_i)$ gradually, with time constant $\tau_m$, while synaptic activation still decays with time constant $\tau$: $$ \dot s_i=-s_i/\tau+r_i+\xi_i, \qquad \tau_m\dot r_i=-r_i+\phi(g_i). $$ Here $\xi_i$ is the zero mean noise from variable spike generation, with the same Poisson strength as in the basic model. **Mathematical derivation.** In this symmetric weight extension, the linear state is $(\delta\mathbf s,\delta\mathbf r)$ and its deterministic matrix is $$ A=\begin{pmatrix} -I/\tau&I\\ \operatorname{diag}(\phi')W/\tau_m&-I/\tau_m \end{pmatrix}. $$ The right tangent is $(\tau\mathbf r',\mathbf r')$. Write the left zero vector as $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)$. The second block of $(\mathbf a^T,\mathbf b^T)A=0$ gives $\mathbf b=\tau_m\mathbf a$. The first then gives $W^T\operatorname{diag}(\phi')\mathbf a=\mathbf a/\tau$, so symmetry again permits $\mathbf a\propto\mathbf g'$. Normalizing its dot product with the right tangent yields $$ a_i=\frac{g_i'}{(\tau+\tau_m)\sum_jg_j'r_j'}. $$ Only the $s$ block receives the modeled spike noise, so $2D=\sum_i a_i^2\bar r_i$. The symmetric formula consequently becomes $$ 2D=\frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {(\tau+\tau_m)^2[\sum_i g_i'r_i']^2}, \qquad 2D\ge\frac{J^{-1}}{(\tau+\tau_m)^2}. $$ **Interpretation.** The sum of the two time constants replaces $\tau$. The larger one dominates when they are very different. This result belongs to the two stage model and noise placement just described; the paper does not prove that arbitrary collections of biological time constants can always be added.[^p1-two-times] **Neural question and model.** The equality condition also depends on the noise law. To see why, replace Poisson spike-count fluctuations with independent additive Gaussian noise of constant strength $q>0$: $$ ds_i=F_i(\mathbf s)dt+\sqrt q\,dB_i. $$ **Mathematical derivation.** The short interval observation of the mean rate is now Gaussian with variance $q/h$. Repeating the score calculation gives $J=\sum_i(r_i')^2/q$, while projection gives $2D=q\sum_i v_i^2$. The same Cauchy Schwarz proof yields $2DJ\ge\tau^{-2}$. Equality requires $v_i\propto r_i'$ because all cells have the same noise strength. In a symmetric network $v_i\propto g_i'$, so a linear transfer rule supplies the condition by keeping $\phi'(g)$ constant across participating inputs. **Interpretation.** In the Poisson case, variance grows with rate and an exponential rule is a sufficient way to attain equality. The pointwise projection condition remains the general criterion, including the [linear-family counterexample](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) already derived. The difference between these sufficient classes follows from the noise weighting, not from linearity being universally preferable.[^p1-gaussian] This explicit $q$ formulation is a teaching reconstruction that keeps dimensions and the noise normalization visible. The supplement's Gaussian subsection establishes the change in equality condition. Here the matched noise and likelihood derivation supplies all factors of $q$ and $\tau$ without requiring the reader to infer a normalization from SI Eqs. S94–S95. ## Readout saturates, and one printed error bound needs qualification {#sec:MEMORY-FIG3-AND-CAUTION} Figure 3 isolates readout uncertainty, rescaling variance by $\sqrt{2D/J}$ and duration by $L^*$. In these axes the ideal curve is $\coth z$ and the naive curve is $z/3+1/z$. Both diverge like $1/z$ at short durations because too few spikes are available. The plotted features are: - The ideal solid curve approaches one. - The naive dashed curve reaches $2/\sqrt3$ at $z=\sqrt3$, then rises because its equal weighting gives increasing importance to displaced states. - The dotted vertical line marks that naive optimum. The storage delay contribution $2DT$ is not part of these rescaled curves. Figure S2 repeats the comparison for partial access, showing the rightward and upward shifts when $\alpha=0.1$.[^p1-fig3]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-3}}
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S2}}
{{block:fig:MEMORY-READOUT-CURVES}}
More observation keeps helping the ideal reader, with diminishing benefit, while equal weighting eventually gives too much influence to a state that has moved. One printed inequality deserves special care. Main Eq. 6 says that total error is at least $2D(T+\tau)$; SI Eq. S83 likewise uses a lower bound with readout term $2D\tau/\sqrt\alpha$. But the paper's other derived results imply $$ 2DJ\ge\tau^{-2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad J\ge\frac1{2D\tau^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt{\frac{2D}{J}}\le2D\tau. $$ Thus the ideal asymptotic readout term is at most $2D\tau$, with equality when the information diffusion inequality is saturated. Substituting an upper bound for this term cannot establish the printed universal lower bound on total error. Within the local Gaussian model, the defensible statement is $$ V_{\mathrm{total}}(T,L) \ge2DT+\sqrt{2D/J}, $$ with equality approached as $L\to\infty$ for the ideal observer. At saturation this asymptotic expression becomes $2D(T+\tau)$. For partial access the same issue occurs with the factor $1/\sqrt\alpha$. This is an apparent inconsistency between printed formulas, identified by algebra using the supplied sources. It is not a claim that the authors issued a correction.[^p1-printed] For a concrete strict inequality case, keep $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$ but set $J=40{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Then $2DJ=400\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ exceeds $\tau^{-2}=100\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The limiting readout variance is $0.0005\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, whereas $2D\tau=0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. At $T=2\,\mathrm{s}$, the Gaussian ideal total limit is $0.0205\,\mathrm{rad}^2$, below $2D(T+\tau)=0.021\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. These values expose the algebraic problem without assuming the bound is saturated. When a continuous attractor circuit is used to accumulate an incoming signal over time, its stored value represents the integral of that signal. The short useful readout interval does not imply a short lifetime for this accumulated value. A tuned circuit can continue to represent the mean of accumulated inputs while its variance grows. A leak would instead pull its mean toward a particular value. [Diffusion limits the accuracy of the integral and the usefulness of long observation; it does not by itself introduce that restoring pull.]{.key-statement} Applying these predictions to an animal also requires checking its spike statistics, tuning, drift, access to spikes, and other sources of movement noise.[^p1-integrator] [^p1-read-setup]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 12, Eq. S57. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-read-gaussian]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 13, Eqs. S58–S63 and the approximation paragraph preceding them. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-naive]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 15–16, Eqs. S76–S81. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The double integral calculation exposes the cross time covariance terms compressed in the printed derivation. [^p1-ideal]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 13–15, Eqs. S58–S75. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The supplement identifies the solution with a reverse Kalman filter. Here the equivalent precision recursion supplies a derivation without assuming prior knowledge of that filter. The printed plus sign in S71 does not match its hyperbolic cosine solution S73; the recursion independently gives the final S75 result. [^p1-time]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, main Eq. 5 and Optimal Observation Time; Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S80–S81. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). [^p1-partial]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 16, Incomplete readout, Eq. S82 and Fig. S2. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The random thinning derivation states when the fraction of spikes equals the fraction of information. [^p1-two-times]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, pp. 17–18, Eqs. S84–S92. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The linear matrix here follows directly from S84; its rate decay block is negative, as required by that differential equation, despite the positive sign printed in the corresponding block of S85. [^p1-gaussian]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text, p. 19, White Gaussian noise, Eqs. S93–S95; main pp. 3–4. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). Constant noise strength $q$ and its likelihood are retained explicitly in the guide's reconstruction. [^p1-fig3]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, Fig. 3, p. 4; Supporting Text, Fig. S2, p. 16. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The caption's readout equation numbers are stale relative to the supplied supplement; the corresponding results are S75 and S79–S81. [^p1-printed]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, main Eqs. 4–6; Supporting Text, Eqs. S75 and S83. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The inequality direction is checked algebraically here, without assuming an author correction or changing the supplied source. [^p1-integrator]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650, Discussion, p. 5; Supporting Text, Integration time constant, p. 17. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109).

# Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings] There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. ## The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time {#sec:EYE-RECORDINGS} The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals; they do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments] The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. [[**Gain**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.]{.definition-explanation} The diagram separates the physical pathway from the paired recordings and the later calculation of predicted eye position.
{{block:fig:EYE-PHYSICAL-AND-RECORDED}}
The upper path describes a possible physical source and its output. The recording design provides one cell and eye movement at a time; it does not measure covariance between simultaneously recorded motor neurons. The predicted position is a later analysis result, not a signal sent backward through the physical pathway. ## A fitted model links movement to firing rate {#sec:EYE-FORWARD-FIT} Position alone does not predict a motor neuron's activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits $$ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). $$ Here $E$ is horizontal eye position in degrees and $\widehat f$ is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold $E_T$ sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units $$ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. $$ Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The delay $\Delta t$ is in seconds: firing at time $t$ predicts movement at the later time $t+\Delta t$ for a positive neural lead. This is the paper's Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.[^p2-forward] The observed rate $f(t)$ was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, $$ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. $$ $a$ labels trials and $T_a$ is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial's rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.[^p2-forward] During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment's mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell; Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. [Its [**p value**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed.]{.definition-explanation} Across 57 cells it gave $p=3\times10^{-9}$. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.[^p2-rate-result] ## A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes {#sec:EYE-INVERSE-FILTER} To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. [The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.]{.key-statement} Let $x(t)=E(t)-E_T$. Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is $$ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. $$ [A [**causal filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its [**impulse response**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $h_0(u)$ is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero.]{.definition-explanation} To factor the equation, consider a time component $e^{pt}$: differentiation multiplies it by $p$. The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is $$ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. $$ Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times $$ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. $$ These are the paired signs in the paper's Eq. 7, with $\tau_+>\tau_-$ when $k,r,m>0$ and $r^2>4km$. In this case both components decay without oscillation. The same factorization gives two useful identities: $$ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. $$ The corresponding impulse response is $$ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). $$ $\Theta(u)$ is zero for $u<0$ and one for $u>0$; it imposes causality. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: $h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)$. Write the spike train as $\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)$, where $\delta$ is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. [The [**convolution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} integral adds the responses to all past spikes.]{.definition-explanation} With spike count treated as a count, $\xi$ has units spikes/s and $h$ has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response; adding those responses produces degrees.[^p2-inversion] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses"} We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as $$ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. $$ To find $A$ and $B$, treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so $h_0(0^+)=0$. Integrating $m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0$ across the pulse gives $m h_0'(0^+)=1$: the velocity changes by $1/m$, while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore $$ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. $$ Substituting $B=-A$ gives $A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m$, hence $A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. # Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 6
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED6}}
There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. ## The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time {#sec:EYE-RECORDINGS} The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals; they do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 7
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED7}}
The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. [[**Gain**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.]{.definition-explanation} The diagram separates the physical pathway from the paired recordings and the later calculation of predicted eye position.
{{block:fig:EYE-PHYSICAL-AND-RECORDED}}
The upper path describes a possible physical source and its output. The recording design provides one cell and eye movement at a time; it does not measure covariance between simultaneously recorded motor neurons. The predicted position is a later analysis result, not a signal sent backward through the physical pathway. ## A fitted model links movement to firing rate {#sec:EYE-FORWARD-FIT} Position alone does not predict a motor neuron's activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits $$ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). $$ Here $E$ is horizontal eye position in degrees and $\widehat f$ is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold $E_T$ sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units $$ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. $$ Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. This is the paper's Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.[^p2-forward] The observed rate $f(t)$ was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell; Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. [Its [**p value**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed.]{.definition-explanation} Across 57 cells it gave $p=3\times10^{-9}$. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.[^p2-rate-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 1

First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is $$ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. $$ [This is the [**coefficient of determination**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for a linear prediction with a fitted gain.]{.definition-explanation} It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ [Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.]{.key-statement}
**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. # Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise {#ch:EYE-TIMING} The shared movement estimate concerns a single interval length. [It leaves open whether the command merely fluctuates around a stable value or keeps accumulating changes. Comparing displacements over different time separations can distinguish these possibilities, but the smallest measured displacements may include a large contribution from recording error.]{.key-statement} The mean squared displacement measures the average squared position change over a chosen interval. Separating the recording error from that quantity is necessary before interpreting its growth. To test whether the command accumulates changes, we compare two possible inputs after a decaying muscle response: fluctuations that do not accumulate and a position that wanders by diffusion. Their different long interval behavior explains how a smooth eye movement can still reflect a wandering stored value. ## Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSD {#sec:EYE-MEASUREMENT-NOISE} The common variance calculation uses one interval length. To learn what kind of process drives motion, the authors next compare displacements at many time separations. Using the [earlier definition of mean squared displacement](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-covariance), $$ M(\ell)=\mathbb E\{[E(t+\ell)-E(t)]^2\} $$ is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag $\ell$. The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.[^p2-msd] At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil's measurement error. Suppose its reading is $E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)$. The measurement error is assumed to have: - Zero mean and variance $\sigma_m^2$. - Independence from true movement. - No correlation between distinct sampled times. For a positive lag, $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm obs}(\ell) &=\mathbb E[(\delta E+\delta\nu)^2]\\ &=M(\ell)+\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)^2]+\mathbb E[\nu(t)^2] -2\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)\nu(t)]\\ &=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed movement-error term vanishes by independence. This is Eqs. 18–19. The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, $2\sigma_m^2$, rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.[^p2-msd-noise] The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order $10^{-3}$ deg$^2$, checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. [This is a correction of an average statistic, not knowledge of each trial's unknown noise.]{.key-statement} Smoothing the eye trajectories instead would also change the movement statistics the analysis seeks to measure. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty $10^{-4}$ deg$^2$, a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. The peer review response uses this example to explain the shortest lag limitation.[^p2-noise-limit] For instance, a constructed measured MSD of $0.0014$ deg$^2$ with an estimated noise contribution $0.0010$ deg$^2$ leaves $0.0004$ deg$^2$. A $0.0001$ deg$^2$ uncertainty in the subtraction is already 25% of that result. This is why a corrected short lag point needs an uncertainty assessment as well as a positive value. If measurement errors were temporally correlated, the correction would instead be $2[\sigma_m^2-C_\nu(\ell)]$, where $C_\nu$ is their covariance at lag $\ell$; a constant subtraction would then need revision. For a constructed Brownian movement with $D=0.010$ deg$^2$/s, adding independent position measurement errors with $2\sigma_m^2=0.0010$ deg$^2$ shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount.
{{block:fig:EYE-MSD-MEASUREMENT-OFFSET}}
The offset comes from two independent position errors, one at each endpoint. Its removal changes the average MSD; it does not recover each trajectory’s unknown error. The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See [Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). ## The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion {#sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD} The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} =\frac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. $$ Ordinary diffusion has $M=2D\ell$ and $\alpha=1$. A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement $v\ell$ and $M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2$, so $\alpha=2$. [Growth faster than linear is called [**superdiffusion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Here it describes a finite range of lags; it does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-msd-result] Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? [A [**low pass filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones.]{.definition-explanation} [[**White noise**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time.]{.definition-explanation} [A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a [**stationary process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation.]{.definition-explanation} Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let $E=h*\xi$, where $$ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). $$ The noise intensity $A$ has units input$^2$ times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for $\ell\ge0$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)] =A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du. $$ For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives $$ M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. $$ If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches $2C_E(0)$, a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.[^p2-white-noise] For the one exponential filter $h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=\frac A\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}). $$ This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to $\ell$ and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing $A$ raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper's simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.[^p2-msd-result] Filtered white noise cannot explain continued long-lag growth. Suppose instead the input is a stored position $B(t)$ undergoing Brownian motion with $\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell$. Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper's full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. Let $$ \tau\dot E+E=B,\qquad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ $W$ is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so $D$ has units deg$^2$/s. Define velocity $v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau$. Taking its increment gives $$ \tau\,dv=-v\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width $h$. The Brownian change $\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)$ has mean zero and variance $h$. Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time $t$ is approximately $(\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j$: the initial change has decayed between $u_j$ and $t$. The integral against $dW(u)$ denotes the limit of these weighted sums as $h$ tends to zero. It does not require an ordinary derivative of the Brownian path. After the initial velocity has decayed, extending the input history into the distant past gives $$ v(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-(t-u)/\tau}\,dW(u). $$ For a lag $s\geq0$, multiply the sums for $v(t)$ and $v(t+s)$ and average. Products of distinct increments have zero mean. The same increment contributes its variance $h$, so the sum becomes an ordinary overlap integral over their shared past: $$ \begin{aligned} C_v(s) &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}\int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-(t-u)/\tau}e^{-(t+s-u)/\tau}\,du\\ &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}e^{-s/\tau}\int_0^\infty e^{-2r/\tau}\,dr =\frac D\tau e^{-s/\tau}. \end{aligned} $$ Here $r=t-u$ is the age of an input increment. Covariance is even in the lag, so $C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}$ for either sign of $s$. Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell) &=\int_0^\ell\int_0^\ell C_v(u-v)\,du\,dv\\ &=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\\ &=2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \end{aligned} $$ At short lags, $1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots$, so $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq(D/\tau)\ell^2. $$ The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags, $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq2D(\ell-\tau), $$ which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau. Its local slope is $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{\ell(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})} {\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})}, $$ approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At $\ell=\tau$ it is $e-1\simeq1.718$; at $\ell=5\tau$ it is about $1.239$. [Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit.]{.key-statement} The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.
{{block:fig:EYE-FILTERED-NOISE-MSD}}
The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example. The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. The one exponential derivation teaches the distinction relevant to Fig. 3: [a decaying low pass filter of stationary white noise saturates, whereas the same filter, with nonzero static gain, retains accumulating displacement from a wandering position. A slow correlated peripheral source is a different hypothesis from the temporally uncorrelated noise rejected by this comparison.]{.key-statement} [^p2-msd]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 10, “Calculation of empirical MSD.” [^p2-msd-noise]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 10, “Removal of measurement noise,” Eqs. 18–19; Supplementary Information, p. 8, Extended Data Fig. 2. The plotted plateau is the displacement noise contribution, twice the single position noise variance. [^p2-noise-limit]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697, peer review file, pp. 20–21, measurement noise subtraction, uncertainty example, and short lag restriction. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). [^p2-msd-result]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 5–6, “Central source” timing argument and Fig. 3. [^p2-white-noise]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 10, “MSD curve of low-pass filtered white noise,” Eqs. 20–22. The normalized one exponential example and filtered Brownian derivation are teaching reconstructions.

For a constructed Brownian movement with $D=0.010$ deg$^2$/s, adding independent position measurement errors with $2\sigma_m^2=0.0010$ deg$^2$ shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount.
