The offset comes from two independent position errors, one at each endpoint. Its removal changes the average MSD; it does not recover each trajectory’s unknown error. The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See [Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). ## The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion {#sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD} The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} =\frac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. $$ Ordinary diffusion has $M=2D\ell$ and $\alpha=1$. A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement $v\ell$ and $M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2$, so $\alpha=2$. [Growth faster than linear is called [**superdiffusion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Here it describes a finite range of lags; it does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-msd-result] Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? [A [**low pass filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones.]{.definition-explanation} [[**White noise**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time.]{.definition-explanation} [A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a [**stationary process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation.]{.definition-explanation} Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let $E=h*\xi$, where $$ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). $$ The noise intensity $A$ has units input$^2$ times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for $\ell\ge0$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)] =A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du. $$ For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives $$ M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. $$ If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches $2C_E(0)$, a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.[^p2-white-noise] For the one exponential filter $h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=\frac A\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}). $$ This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to $\ell$ and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing $A$ raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper's simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.[^p2-msd-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-3}}
Filtered white noise cannot explain continued long-lag growth. Suppose instead the input is a stored position $B(t)$ undergoing Brownian motion with $\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell$. Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper's full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. Let $$ \tau\dot E+E=B,\qquad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ $W$ is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so $D$ has units deg$^2$/s. Define velocity $v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau$. Taking its increment gives $$ \tau\,dv=-v\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width $h$. The Brownian change $\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)$ has mean zero and variance $h$. Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time $t$ is approximately $(\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j$: the initial change has decayed between $u_j$ and $t$. The integral against $dW(u)$ denotes the limit of these weighted sums as $h$ tends to zero. It does not require an ordinary derivative of the Brownian path. After the initial velocity has decayed, extending the input history into the distant past gives $$ v(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-(t-u)/\tau}\,dW(u). $$ For a lag $s\geq0$, multiply the sums for $v(t)$ and $v(t+s)$ and average. Products of distinct increments have zero mean. The same increment contributes its variance $h$, so the sum becomes an ordinary overlap integral over their shared past: $$ \begin{aligned} C_v(s) &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}\int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-(t-u)/\tau}e^{-(t+s-u)/\tau}\,du\\ &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}e^{-s/\tau}\int_0^\infty e^{-2r/\tau}\,dr =\frac D\tau e^{-s/\tau}. \end{aligned} $$ Here $r=t-u$ is the age of an input increment. Covariance is even in the lag, so $C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}$ for either sign of $s$. Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell) &=\int_0^\ell\int_0^\ell C_v(u-v)\,du\,dv\\ &=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\\ &=2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \end{aligned} $$ At short lags, $1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots$, so $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq(D/\tau)\ell^2. $$ The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags, $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq2D(\ell-\tau), $$ which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau. Its local slope is $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{\ell(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})} {\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})}, $$ approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At $\ell=\tau$ it is $e-1\simeq1.718$; at $\ell=5\tau$ it is about $1.239$. [Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit.]{.key-statement} The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.
{{block:fig:EYE-FILTERED-NOISE-MSD}}

The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. edits.old: # A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift {#ch:EYE-CIRCUIT} The recordings support a shared source before the motor neurons, and the movement's timing is compatible with a stored position that wanders. [Neither result identifies the circuit that supplies that command. A noisy memory circuit is a proposed explanation whose output must pass through the motor neurons and muscles before it can be compared with eye movement.]{.key-statement} Following that complete path lets the model test whether neural noise can produce both the amount and timing of the observed drift. Its spike variability, neuron count and time constants determine how much freedom this match allows. Comparing the model with the separate recording and timing results then shows what the study supports, and why it still leaves other upstream sources possible. ## A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering {#sec:EYE-CIRCUIT-MODEL} The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right; the other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.[^p2-network] For the right population, the model's rate is $$ \lambda_i^R(t)=\left[\zeta_i^R E_{OI}(t)+\lambda_i^0+\zeta_i^R F(t)\right]_+, \qquad [a]_+=\max(a,0). $$ $E_{OI}$ is the internally represented position in degrees, $\zeta_i^R$ is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and $\lambda_i^0$ is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. $F$ is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, $\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R$. In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by $\zeta_i$. The model scales each spike train into an input $X_i$ with a saturating mean response. This input changes the neuron's synaptic output $S_i$, the lingering effect of its spikes on neurons receiving them. A weighted difference between the two groups' synaptic outputs gives the represented eye angle $E_{OI}$. This value sets the firing rates again, closing the feedback loop: $$ \tau_s\dot S_i^R=-S_i^R+X_i^R,\qquad X_i^R(t)=\frac{\xi_i^R(t)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(t)},\qquad E_{OI}(t)=\sum_i\eta_i[S_i^R(t)-S_i^L(t)]. $$ Here $\xi_i^R$ is a spike train generated at rate $\lambda_i^R$, $\tau_s$ is the synaptic decay time, and $\lambda_t=60$ Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, $X_i$ and $S_i$ are dimensionless, and the weights $\eta_i$ are in degrees. Between spikes, $S_i$ decays exponentially; one spike adds a jump of $1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]$. Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive $\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)$ that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model's saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.[^p2-network] Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set $F=0$ and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value $z$ by $$ q_i^R(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^R(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(z)}, \qquad q_i^L(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^L(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^L(z)}. $$ Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same $\tau_s$ applies to every unit, the readout obeys $$ \tau_s\dot E_{OI}=-E_{OI}+G(E_{OI}), \qquad G(z)=\sum_i\eta_i[q_i^R(z)-q_i^L(z)]. $$ [An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require $G(z)=z$ over the represented range.]{.key-statement} For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives $$ \tau_s\,\frac{d\,\delta E_{OI}}{dt} =[G'(z)-1]\delta E_{OI}. $$ Thus $G'(z)=1$ is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across $-50$ to $50$ degrees. [Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum.]{.key-statement} The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction additionally accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper's equations; Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.[^p2-network] The motor neurons receive this position signal: $$ \lambda_i^M(t)=[k_i(E_{OI}(t)-E_{T_i})]_+, \qquad \tau_{MN}\dot s_i^M=-s_i^M+\xi_i^M. $$ $\lambda_i^M$ is a motor rate in spikes/s, $E_{T_i}$ is that neuron's position threshold in degrees, and $k_i$ is its position sensitivity. $\xi_i^M$ is its generated spike train. The filtered output $s_i^M$ also has units spikes/s, with decay time $\tau_{MN}$. One spike makes a jump of $1/\tau_{MN}$; at constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate. Each motor unit's muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution $E_i$ satisfying $$ s_i^M=k_i(E_i-E_{T_i})+r_i\dot E_i+m_i\ddot E_i, \qquad E=\frac1{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}E_i. $$ These are Eqs. 28–31. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant $E_{OI}$, an active unit has mean $s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})$, giving mean $E_i=E_{OI}$ when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.[^p2-motor] The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between $-45$ and $-5$ degrees, and imposed $m_i {{block:tbl:EYE-FIGURE-GUIDE}} The most useful supplemental comparisons are Extended Data Fig. 1 for individual uncertainty, Fig. 2 for noise subtraction and its simulated control, Fig. 3 for feedback, Fig. 4 for a no-central-drive control, and Fig. 5 for the other monkey's fit. In the no-central-drive control, $\widehat\chi=-0.09\pm0.22$ is compatible with zero; that negative estimate is sampling variation. Figures 6–8 document cell classification, segment sampling, and a rank correlation check. Figure 9 shows the heterogeneous model parameters. Figure 10 separates spiking noise passed directly to the output from spiking noise that drives diffusion inside the integrator: internal stochastic spikes remain in the latter comparison. Its caption reports little direct output-noise effect beyond 50 ms.[^p2-supp-figures] ## The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit {#sec:EYE-LIMITS} The data and model answer different questions about where the drive originates: - The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions. - The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter. - The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing. Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. Two missing tests limit that conclusion: - No integrator neurons were recorded in this study. - No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift. [Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.]{.key-statement}[^p2-localization] The study's empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. To compare a memory theory with behavior, the mapping from stored value to measured movement is part of the calculation. [^p2-network]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 10–11, “Oculomotor integrator network,” Eqs. 23–27; Supplementary Information, p. 13, Extended Data Fig. 9. [^p2-motor]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 11, “OMN activity and actual eye position,” Eqs. 28–33 and simulation parameters; p. 6, Fig. 3 caption, private OMN comparison. [^p2-feedback]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 7, 9, 11, “Visual feedback,” Eq. 34; Supplementary Information, pp. 4–5 and p. 9, Extended Data Fig. 3. Some supplement cross references use earlier figure/equation numbers; p. 5 also mentions 15K integrator neurons, whereas final main Methods specify 30,000. This guide uses final main paper numbering and its main simulation parameters. [^p2-cv]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 11, “Sub-Poisson spike trains,” Eq. 35 and integrator variability specification. The interval-sum derivation expands the construction given there. [^p2-scaling]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 6, Eq. 1 and its parameter discussion; peer review file, p. 23, changes in slope, synaptic time constant, and neuron count. The absolute versus fractional slope distinction is the guide's dimensional interpretation of the printed normalization ambiguity, connected to the guide’s diffusion and information calculations. [^p2-cv-drift]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Supplementary Information, pp. 2–3, “Contribution of oculomotor state to the CV of OMNs,” Eqs. S3–S6. Intermediate covariance integrals and numerical evaluation are expanded here. [^p2-supp-figures]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697, Supplementary Information, pp. 7–14, Extended Data Figs. 1–10. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). The no-central-drive result is Extended Data Fig. 4, p. 10; the output-noise comparison is Extended Data Fig. 10, p. 14. [^p2-localization]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one; the model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. [Such firing is called [**sub-Poisson spiking**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-cv] The construction starts with a Poisson process at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of $M$ independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean $1/(M\lambda)$ and variance $1/(M\lambda)^2$. The retained interval therefore has mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/(M\lambda^2)$, and CV $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model; the simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate. At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. [This is a [**renewal process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed.]{.definition-explanation} Let their mean be $\mu=1/\lambda$ and standard deviation $\sigma_I$. The time to $n$ spikes has variance $n\sigma_I^2$. For a long fixed window $L\simeq n\mu$, a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by $\mu$. Thus $$ \operatorname{Var}(n)\simeq\frac{n\sigma_I^2}{\mu^2} \simeq\lambda L\left(\frac{\sigma_I}{\mu}\right)^2 =\lambda L\,\mathrm{CV}^2. $$ This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The [diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) and [information bound](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to $1/\tau_s^2$ and, for a comparable independent population, $1/N$. Rate and sensitivity need more care. Write the absolute local rate slope as $a=d\lambda/dE$, in spikes/(s deg). If $N$ similar cells fire near rate $\lambda_0$, their Poisson information per unit time about position is $$ J\simeq\frac{Na^2}{\lambda_0}. $$ Using the [information-diffusion relation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) as a scale, including the $\mathrm{CV}^2$ factor just derived and holding the network geometry fixed, $$ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{\tau_s^2J} =\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{N a^2\tau_s^2}. $$ If instead sensitivity is expressed as the fractional slope $b=a/\lambda_0$, in inverse degrees, the same expression becomes $$ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2}. $$ This second form has the dependence printed in the paper's Eq. 1, $D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2N^{-1}\lambda_0^{-1}k_0^{-2}\tau_s^{-2}$. However, its surrounding text calls $k_0$ position sensitivity without specifying fractional normalization. If $k_0$ means an absolute slope in Hz/degree, that printed expression has the wrong units for $D$; the version with $\lambda_0$ in the numerator has the required units deg$^2$/s. This scaling is a comparison under fixed network geometry and noise assumptions, not an exact formula for every recurrent circuit.[^p2-scaling] At fixed network geometry and under the noise assumptions above, the scale changes as follows: - Doubling $N$ halves it. - Doubling CV multiplies it by four. - Doubling $\tau_s$ divides it by four. - Doubling the absolute slope at fixed rate also divides it by four. [Increasing rate reduces diffusion when the fractional slope is fixed, because more spikes then also supply a proportionally steeper absolute slope. Increasing rate at fixed absolute slope is a different comparison and increases the scale in the first formula. A rate change alone does not specify which comparison is intended.]{.key-statement} Could the measured CV itself mostly reflect drift rather than private spike variability? Supplementary Notes test this. Let $\lambda(t)=\bar\lambda+aB(t)$ during a fixation of length $T$, with the rate changes small relative to $\bar\lambda$. For a Brownian path starting at zero, the expected time averaged squared position is $DT$, and the expected squared time mean is $2DT/3$. Subtracting gives the expected within-segment position variance $DT/3=2DT/6$: $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T(B(t)-\bar B)^2dt\right] =\frac{DT}{3}. $$ The second term follows from $\mathbb E[B(t)B(s)]=2D\min(t,s)$ and $T^{-2}\int_0^T\int_0^T2D\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds=2DT/3$. Expanding $1/(\bar\lambda+aB)$ to first order gives $1/\bar\lambda-aB/\bar\lambda^2$. Dividing its standard deviation by its mean then gives $$ \mathrm{CV}_{\rm drift}\simeq \frac{|a|}{\bar\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{2DT}{6}}. $$ With the supplement's values $a=1/15$ spikes/(s arcmin), $2D=100$ arcmin$^2$/s, $T=0.5$ s, and $\bar\lambda=80$ Hz, this is about $0.0024$, well below the OMN CV near 0.07. These are an order of magnitude check, not a fitted diffusion constant for the whole model. Since one degree is 60 arcmin, that $2D$ equals $0.0278$ deg$^2$/s, or $D=0.0139$ deg$^2$/s.[^p2-cv-drift] ## The figures test shared drive, diffusion, and the full circuit model {#sec:EYE-FIGURES} The five figures address different steps. Their agreement is easier to assess when those questions remain separate.
{{block:tbl:EYE-FIGURE-GUIDE}}
The most useful supplemental comparisons are Extended Data Fig. 1 for individual uncertainty, Fig. 2 for noise subtraction and its simulated control, Fig. 3 for feedback, Fig. 4 for a no-central-drive control, and Fig. 5 for the other monkey's fit. In the no-central-drive control, $\widehat\chi=-0.09\pm0.22$ is compatible with zero; that negative estimate is sampling variation. Figures 6–8 document cell classification, segment sampling, and a rank correlation check. Figure 9 shows the heterogeneous model parameters. Figure 10 separates spiking noise passed directly to the output from spiking noise that drives diffusion inside the integrator: internal stochastic spikes remain in the latter comparison. Its caption reports little direct output-noise effect beyond 50 ms.[^p2-supp-figures]

## The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit {#sec:EYE-LIMITS} The data and model answer different questions about where the drive originates: - The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions. - The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter. - The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing. Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. Two missing tests limit that conclusion: - No integrator neurons were recorded in this study. - No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift. [Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.]{.key-statement}[^p2-localization] The study's empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. To compare a memory theory with behavior, the mapping from stored value to measured movement is part of the calculation. [^p2-network]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. # Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale {#ch:PLACE-FIELDS} The study compares recordings of hippocampal place cells from bats flying through tunnels, rats moving over an arena floor, and bats flying through a room. For tunnel flights, the analysis uses distance along an approximately one-dimensional route, although the tunnel itself has width and height. The floor map uses two position coordinates, and the room map uses three. A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. [On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?]{.key-statement} Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. This function can be interpreted as the average combined input arriving through the cell's synapses at each animal position. The model cell has positive firing rate where this input exceeds a threshold. The recordings estimate firing rates rather than measuring this input directly.[^p3-model] [The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question] We begin on a track, where a field starts at [an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold.]{.definition-explanation} Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes. [Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement} ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. [A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector.]{.definition-explanation} For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, $$ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. $$ The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. [A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model] Three assumptions have different jobs: - [[**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not say that a particular map is flat. - [[**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$.]{.definition-explanation} It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. - [[**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives.]{.definition-explanation} Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, $$ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). $$ Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model] [The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.]{.key-statement} For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). $$ The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale $$ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. $$ Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$.
{{block:fig:PLACE-GP-TO-FIRING}}
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13). ## Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction {#sec:PLACE-KAC-RICE} A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root. Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing $x_0$ of $q$, with slope $v=z'(x_0)>0$. Close to the crossing, $$ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). $$ The curve lies in the vertical band $|z-q|<\varepsilon$ for a spatial distance approximately $2\varepsilon/v$. Integrating $z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)$ over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. [Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the [**Kac–Rice formula**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for the mean upcrossing density,]{.definition-explanation} $$ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. $$ The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.[^p3-crossings] A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
{{block:fig:PLACE-CROSSINGS}}
The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention. We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives $$ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. $$ Height and slope are jointly Gaussian; zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})$. Consequently, $$ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ In the integral, use $u=\sigma^2v^2/2$, so $v\,dv=du/\sigma^2$. [This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed.]{.key-statement} Its units are inverse distance: increasing $\sigma$ stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. On a finite track $[0,L]$, each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If $N_L$ counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings, $$ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), $$ where $Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper's exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8.[^p3-ec-source] ## Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale {#sec:PLACE-INFERENCE} [A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.]{.key-statement} At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$. Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$. On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means] Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time: $$ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). $$ Thus $$ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. $$ For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings. [The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent. Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives $$ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. $$ The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.[^p3-selection] [^p3-question]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., & Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Introduction and Results, pp. 1110–1111; Figure 1. [^p3-model]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), STAR Methods, Equations 2–3, p. e1; Supplemental Methods S1, p. 8. [^p3-scale]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), STAR Methods, Equation 4, p. e2; Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S10–S11. The derivative calculation here is expanded for teaching. [^p3-crossings]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S9–S13, pp. 10–11. The narrow-band upcrossing argument is a reconstruction. See also Mainali, N. (2026, August 6), *Mathematical properties of Gaussian process neural code: Excursion geometry, spectral structure, and coding error*, [author teaching notes, “The Kac-Rice formula” and “Expected crossing count”](https://nischmainali.github.io/blog/gp-code-notes/). [^p3-ec-source]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Figure 3F–H; STAR Methods, “Euler characteristics,” Equations 8–10, p. e3. [^p3-means]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S14–S15; STAR Methods, “Parameter inference in 1D environments.” The explicit inversion is derived here. [^p3-selection]: Mainali et al. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.]{.key-statement}[^p3-question] We begin on a track, where a field starts at [an [**upcrossing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a point where the input crosses upward through the threshold.]{.definition-explanation} Counting these crossings gives the average number of fields. Combining that count with the lengths of active fields and inactive gaps then separates the effect of the threshold from the distance over which the map changes. These calculations establish the parameters needed for the later predictions of sizes and shapes. [Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning.]{.key-statement} ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. [A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector.]{.definition-explanation} For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, $$ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. $$ The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. These two functions determine every finite joint distribution. A Gaussian process can thus produce many different curves while keeping a precise rule for their spatial dependence. [A [**jointly Gaussian vector**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is one for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian.]{.definition-explanation} For this family, zero covariance between two subvectors implies their independence. That extra property, which does not hold for general distributions, will simplify the crossing calculation. The values after thresholding will generally not have a Gaussian distribution.[^p3-model] Three assumptions have different jobs: - [[**Stationarity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that moving the observation window does not change the map's probability law. Here it gives a constant mean and a covariance $C(x,y)=C(y-x)$ that depends on separation.]{.definition-explanation} It does not say that a particular map is flat. - [[**Isotropy**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means that rotating the separation does not change the covariance: in several dimensions, $C(\Delta x)$ depends only on $\|\Delta x\|$.]{.definition-explanation} It rules out a preferred direction in the model's statistics. Stationarity alone does not imply isotropy. - [[**Smoothness**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} controls whether the map has well defined spatial derivatives.]{.definition-explanation} Crossing calculations require differentiable sample functions and nondegenerate joint distributions: the relevant vector of heights and derivatives must have an invertible covariance matrix, rather than obey an exact linear constraint. Peak calculations require second derivatives and enough regularity to control their local approximation. A Gaussian distribution of values does not guarantee this smoothness. For example, a covariance proportional to $e^{-|x-y|/b}$ has a sharp corner at zero separation and does not supply the differentiable paths assumed below. Set the mean to zero and write $\sigma_h^2=C(0)$ for input variance. A constant input mean can be absorbed into the threshold. It is useful to normalize the input, $$ z(x)=\frac{h(x)}{\sigma_h},\qquad F(x)=a\,[z(x)-q]_+, \quad [u]_+=\max(u,0). $$ Here $z$ has variance one, $q$ is a dimensionless threshold, and $a>0$ converts normalized input to firing rate, in Hz. The paper writes $\theta$ for $q$, $r$ for covariance, and $D$ for spatial dimension; this guide uses $q,C,d$ to avoid conflicts with earlier chapters. The original input threshold is $q\sigma_h$. In the paper's Equation 3 the firing rate is proportional to $[h-q\sigma_h]_+$, which is equivalent to this form after choosing the gain.[^p3-model]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-1}}
[The [**excursion set**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} above $q$ is]{.definition-explanation} $$ A_q=\{x:z(x)>q\}. $$ Each connected piece of $A_q$ is a model place field. In one dimension its size is length. In two and three dimensions it is area and volume. [Two nearby peaks belong to one field if an above-threshold path joins them. Counting peaks and counting fields therefore answer different questions.]{.key-statement} For a one dimensional stationary process, differentiation of covariance gives $$ \operatorname{Var}(h')= \left.\partial_x\partial_y C(y-x)\right|_{y=x}=-C''(0). $$ The minus sign comes from differentiating $y-x$ once with respect to each variable. The paper defines the spatial scale $$ \sigma=\sqrt{-\frac{C(0)}{C''(0)}}; \qquad \operatorname{Var}(z')=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}. $$ Thus $\sigma$ compares typical height with typical slope and has units of distance. In an isotropic field, the same definition applies along any unit direction. For the smooth Gaussian covariance $C(\Delta x)=\sigma_h^2\exp[-\|\Delta x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)]$, it is exactly the parameter in that exponent. The paper uses a Gaussian covariance for its simulations. Other smooth covariances can share this local scale while having different longer distance structure.[^p3-scale] A simulated Gaussian input map with covariance $C(\Delta x)=\exp[-(\Delta x/\sigma)^2/2]$ gives the firing map below when $q=0.8$ and $a=6$ Hz. Position is shown in units of $\sigma$.
{{block:fig:PLACE-GP-TO-FIRING}}
Thresholding changes the distribution of values and can separate one smooth input curve into several fields. Both panels describe the same fixed map over space, so neither curve is a trajectory over time. See [Gaussian input and firing rate, STAR Methods Eqs. 2–3, p. e1](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=13). ## Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction {#sec:PLACE-KAC-RICE} A field starts at an upcrossing, so its expected count can be found by counting upward passages through the threshold. A small interval around each crossing has a width determined by its slope; this lets us count crossings without locating every root. Consider a differentiable fixed curve and a simple upward crossing $x_0$ of $q$, with slope $v=z'(x_0)>0$. Close to the crossing, $$ z(x)-q\simeq v(x-x_0). $$ The curve lies in the vertical band $|z-q|<\varepsilon$ for a spatial distance approximately $2\varepsilon/v$. Integrating $z'(x)/(2\varepsilon)$ over that interval contributes one. Restricting to positive slopes counts only upward crossings. [Under the usual regularity conditions, averaging this counting identity gives the [**Kac–Rice formula**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for the mean upcrossing density,]{.definition-explanation} $$ \nu_+(q)=\int_0^\infty v\,p_{z,z'}(q,v)\,dv. $$ The density $p_{z,z'}(q,v)$ describes how often height is near $q$ and slope near $v$. Multiplication by $v$ compensates for the shorter spatial window of a steep crossing. Multiplying the probability of being above threshold by a typical slope would miss this weighting.[^p3-crossings] A fixed smooth curve shows how to count a field already active at the left edge and why the crossing integral weights each slope.
{{block:fig:PLACE-CROSSINGS}}
The count includes every connected active interval intersecting the track. Discarding clipped boundary fields would change this convention. We can evaluate the integral because height and slope are independent here. Stationarity gives $$ \mathbb E[zz']=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb E[z(x)^2]=0. $$ Height and slope are jointly Gaussian; zero covariance therefore makes them independent. Their distributions are $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $z'\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2})$. Consequently, $$ \begin{aligned} \nu_+(q) &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^\infty v\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\sigma^2v^2/2}\,dv\\ &=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} =\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma}. \end{aligned} $$ In the integral, use $u=\sigma^2v^2/2$, so $v\,dv=du/\sigma^2$. [This result is exact for the stated smooth stationary Gaussian model. A high threshold is not needed.]{.key-statement} Its units are inverse distance: increasing $\sigma$ stretches the map and reduces crossings per metre. On a finite track $[0,L]$, each upcrossing starts a field, but a field may already be active at the left endpoint. If $N_L$ counts all components intersecting the track, then, under regularity conditions that exclude tangencies and give nonzero slopes at crossings, $$ N_L=N_+(q;[0,L])+\mathbf1\{z(0)>q\}, \qquad \mathbb E[N_L]=L\nu_+(q)+Q(q), $$ where $Q(q)=1-\Phi(q)$ and $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The last term is the endpoint correction. Removing incomplete boundary fields changes the counting convention, so the same correction cannot then be used unchanged. This identity also gives the paper's exact one dimensional mean Euler characteristic, Equation 8.[^p3-ec-source] ## Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale {#sec:PLACE-INFERENCE} [A low field count can result from a high threshold or a slowly varying map. Field lengths help separate those possibilities.]{.key-statement} At a uniformly chosen position, the probability of activity is $Q(q)$. Hence a track of length $L$ has expected occupied length $LQ(q)$. On a long stationary track, the average occupied length per field is the occupied length per unit distance divided by the number of fields per unit distance. The corresponding gap calculation uses the inactive fraction $\Phi(q)$: $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_s&=\frac{Q(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma Q(q)e^{q^2/2},\\ \mu_g&=\frac{\Phi(q)}{\nu_+(q)} =2\pi\sigma\Phi(q)e^{q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These are stationary per-field and per-gap means, ignoring clipping at track boundaries. They are not an assertion that the expectation of a finite sample's ratio equals the ratio of its expectations. Subject to suitable averaging over a long track or many maps, they give the inference rule in Methods S3, Equations S14–S15.[^p3-means] Adding and dividing removes one unknown at a time: $$ \mu_s+\mu_g=2\pi\sigma e^{q^2/2},\qquad \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_s+\mu_g}=Q(q). $$ Thus $$ q=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mu_g}{\mu_s+\mu_g}\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{\mu_s+\mu_g}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2}. $$ For example, $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m, the fitted parameters reported for the 200 m bat tunnel, give $Q(q)=0.1357$, $\nu_+=0.03621$ per metre, $\mu_s=3.746$ m, and $\mu_g=23.868$ m in the continuous model. Putting these two means into the inversion recovers $q=1.1$ and $\sigma=2.4$ m. The expected number of intersecting fields on a 200 m track is $7.2425+0.1357=7.3782$, including the left endpoint term. These are calculations from the fitted model, not fresh estimates from raw recordings. [The means do not imply a full gap or count distribution. At high thresholds, distant rare excursions can approach independent events if correlations decay sufficiently with distance. In that regime, field locations approach a Poisson process, counts in a long interval are approximately Poisson, and gaps are approximately exponential. Smoothness and stationarity alone do not ensure this independence.]{.key-statement} A periodic Gaussian process, for example, retains long distance dependence. Upward and downward crossings that enclose the same small field remain strongly related even when fields far apart are almost independent. Experimental selection also matters. If cells with no fields are excluded, a Poisson model with unconditioned mean $\lambda$ gives $$ \Pr(N=n\mid N\ge1)= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!(1-e^{-\lambda})},\quad n\ge1, \qquad \mathbb E[N\mid N\ge1]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}. $$ The mean follows because the omitted $n=0$ term contributes zero to $\sum n\Pr(N=n)=\lambda$, while conditioning divides all remaining probabilities by $1-e^{-\lambda}$. For $\lambda=1$, $36.8\%$ of cells are excluded and the observed mean is $1.582$, not one. Using $1.582$ as the unconditioned mean would infer too many fields. The paper applies this correction to its two dimensional count fit, Equation 5.[^p3-selection] [^p3-question]: Mainali, N., Azeredo da Silveira, R., & Burak, Y. (2025). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Introduction and Results, pp. 1110–1111; Figure 1. [^p3-model]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), STAR Methods, Equations 2–3, p. e1; Supplemental Methods S1, p. 8. The derivative calculation here is expanded for teaching. [^p3-crossings]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Supplemental Methods S3, Equations S9–S13, pp. 10–11. [^p3-ec-source]: Mainali et al. # High peaks explain size laws across dimensions {#ch:PLACE-SIZES} [Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often very small or very large fields occur. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room?]{.key-statement} The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold. Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement} We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$. ## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: - a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field; - an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables; - the limit $q\to\infty$; - typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$; the remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. At fixed $u\ge0$ and as $q$ increases, $$ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. $$ [Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one.]{.key-statement} In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor $q^{d-1}$. Its ratio at $q+u/q$ and $q$ tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the [Euler characteristic calculation](ch-place-tests.html#sec-place-topology). A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is $s=2r_*$. Eliminating $\epsilon$ gives $$ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. $$ This supplies two distinct predictions: - [The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a [**Rayleigh distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} - The peak firing rate is $a\epsilon$, so at fixed high $q$ it is proportional to $s^2$. The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is $s^{1/3}$ when $s$ denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of $1.42$ in the 200 m bat data and $1.46$ in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports $1.75$ versus $1.71$ using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large; they are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as $q$ increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.[^p3-shapes] ## Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension {#sec:PLACE-SIZE-LAW} A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let $v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)$ be the volume of a unit ball in $d$ dimensions. For $d=1,2,3$, it is $2,\pi,4\pi/3$. [The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-DENSITY-COLLAPSE}}
Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference; its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See [Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=3).
{{block:tbl:PLACE-SIZE-LAWS}}
[A [**Weibull distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} has survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$ for size $s>0$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation} Here $k=2/d$ and $b=\beta^{-d/2}$. In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of $00. $$ The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. [This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of $q$ under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation.]{.key-statement} Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is $av$, so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.[^p3-slope-source] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope"} There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope $v$, the local excursion is approximately $$ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. $$ Its second root is $s=2\sigma^2v/q$. Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives $p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}$ with $\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)$, the same constant as the peak calculation for $v_1=2$. ::: Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input. [^p3-rare-source]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Supplemental Methods S4, pp. 12–14, especially Equations S22–S25. The supplement cites Adler (1981) for the peak approximation. The main article cites Nosko (1988), reference 32, for asymptotic field statistics. This chapter supplies a local derivation and does not claim to reproduce either full theorem proof. [^p3-shapes]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Figures 3C–D, 4C, 5A–C, pp. 1115–1117; STAR Methods, “Maximum firing rate vs. field width.” The gain is matched through the fitted log-log intercept. [^p3-size-source]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), main Equation 1 and Supplemental Methods S3–S4. The isotropic ball calculation and its explicit leading $\beta$ are reconstructed here. [^p3-corrections]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), supplement printed pp. 12–14, Equations S18, S22–S25. Direct inspection of the PDF confirms these are printed expressions rather than text-extraction errors. The corrected constants also reproduce the large-$q$ limit of S14. [^p3-slices-source]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Figure 2 and “Place fields in two and three dimensions,” pp. 1113–1114; Figure S2A–C, supplemental p. 2. Sampling distinctions follow from restricting the process and are explained here. [^p3-slope-source]: Mainali et al. (2025), *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*, Neuron, 113, 1110–1120.e3, [doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017), Figure 3E, p. 1115; STAR Methods, “Boundary slopes.” The derivation is reconstructed from crossing counts. Mainali's [author teaching notes, “Slope at an upcrossing”](https://nischmainali.github.io/blog/gp-code-notes/), give the same slope weighting.
