Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. [The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions.]{.key-statement} We keep the earlier notation: $z(x)$ is the spatial input normalized to variance one, $q$ is its threshold, $\sigma$ is its local distance scale, and $a$ converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$. The firing rule remains $F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+$, where $[u]_+=\max(u,0)$. ## Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic {#sec:PLACE-RARE-PEAKS} The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: - a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field; - an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables; - the limit $q\to\infty$; - typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.[^p3-rare-source] [The [**Hessian**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix $H$ of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions.]{.definition-explanation} Isotropy and the definition of $\sigma$ imply $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. $$ Here $\delta_{ij}$ is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning $Y$ on a scalar $Z$ of variance one gives $\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b$ when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write $Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon$; the remainder has zero covariance with $Z$ and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives $$ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. $$ The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with $b$. For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order $q$, so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be $q+\epsilon$, with $\epsilon>0$, and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, $$ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. $$ It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius $$ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. $$ The remaining question is how $\epsilon$ is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to $e^{-q^2/2}$. Therefore the fraction of peaks above $q$ that also exceed $q+\epsilon$ is approximately $$ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. $$ Define $U=q\epsilon$. At fixed $u\ge0$ and as $q$ increases, $$ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. $$ [Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one.]{.key-statement} In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor $q^{d-1}$. Its ratio at $q+u/q$ and $q$ tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the [Euler characteristic calculation](ch-place-tests.html#sec-place-topology). A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is $s=2r_*$. Eliminating $\epsilon$ gives $$ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. $$ This supplies two distinct predictions: - [The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a [**Rayleigh distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} - The peak firing rate is $a\epsilon$, so at fixed high $q$ it is proportional to $s^2$. The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is $s^{1/3}$ when $s$ denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of $1.42$ in the 200 m bat data and $1.46$ in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports $1.75$ versus $1.71$ using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large; they are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as $q$ increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.[^p3-shapes]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 5
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-5}}
## Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension {#sec:PLACE-SIZE-LAW} A round region's radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let $v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)$ be the volume of a unit ball in $d$ dimensions. For $d=1,2,3$, it is $2,\pi,4\pi/3$. [The symbol $\Gamma$ is the [**gamma function**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, defined for $t>0$ by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du$. It extends factorials: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$.]{.definition-explanation} Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is $$ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. $$ The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-GEOMETRY}}
The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of $U$ is $e^{-u}$ for $u>0$, changing variables gives $$ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} $$ This is the paper's Equation 1. The expression for $\beta$ above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.[^p3-size-source] The mean and its corresponding scale are $$ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: normalization and higher size moments"} Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment, $$ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). $$ ::: Size has units of distance to the power $d$, while $\beta$ has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes $\beta s^{2/d}$ dimensionless, and makes $p_d(s)$ a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as $w=\beta^{d/2}s$ removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable $U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}$ has the same exponential law.
{{block:fig:PLACE-SIZE-DENSITY-COLLAPSE}}
Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference; its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See [Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf#page=3).
{{block:tbl:PLACE-SIZE-LAWS}}
[A [**Weibull distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} has survival probability $\exp[-(s/b)^k]$ for size $s>0$, scale $b>0$, and shape $k>0$.]{.definition-explanation} Here $k=2/d$ and $b=\beta^{-d/2}$. In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of $0 Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-2}}
[The dashed analytical curves change with the dimension of the measurement, even within one recorded map. The alternative spherical-field model in Figure S2 matches empirical volumes and peak rates by construction but fails these slice distributions and the topology test. Matching volumes alone is therefore insufficient.]{.key-statement}[^p3-slices-source]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S2
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S2}}
## Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh {#sec:PLACE-SLOPES} The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution. Return to the [crossing integral](ch-place-fields.html#sec-place-kac-rice) and retain only slopes between $v$ and $v+dv$. Their contribution is proportional to $v p_{z'}(v)dv$. Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing: $$ p_{\uparrow}(v) =\frac{v p_{z'}(v)}{\int_0^\infty w p_{z'}(w)\,dw} =\sigma^2v\exp[-\sigma^2v^2/2],\qquad v>0. $$ The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. [This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of $q$ under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation.]{.key-statement} Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is $av$, so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.[^p3-slope-source] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope"} There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope $v$, the local excursion is approximately $$ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. $$ Its second root is $s=2\sigma^2v/q$. Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives $p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}$ with $\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)$, the same constant as the peak calculation for $v_1=2$. ::: Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input.
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-3}}

# Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation {#ch:PLACE-TESTS} [Two maps can have the same field sizes and counts while arranging their active regions differently. One may contain rings or tunnels that the other lacks. Can the Gaussian spatial model account for these differences, and how much would that agreement tell us about the circuit that produced the maps?]{.key-statement} We first count connected regions and holes together, which gives a prediction across activity thresholds. The boundary of the observed environment matters for this calculation, so we keep its contributions. We then examine which measured quantities set the model's parameters and which provide further tests. Finally, a sum of many randomly weighted inputs shows one way a circuit could produce Gaussian spatial input, while making clear which assumptions and circuit measurements that explanation still needs. The map is still fixed over space. As before, $q$ is the normalized activity threshold, $\sigma$ is the local spatial scale, and $a$ converts normalized input above threshold into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$; it is separate from the diffusion coefficient $D$ used in the memory chapters. ## Holes distinguish maps with the same field count {#sec:PLACE-TOPOLOGY} Two maps can have the same field count and total active area but different holes. As the activity threshold rises, active regions shrink and can split or disappear. The numbers of components and holes can change. [The [**Euler characteristic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\chi$, combines these counts differently in each dimension:]{.definition-explanation} - In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals. - In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have $\chi=3$; one connected ring has $\chi=1-1=0$. - In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has $\chi=1$, a solid ring has $\chi=0$, and a hollow spherical shell has $\chi=2$. [These counts are the first three [**Betti numbers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.]{.definition-explanation}[^p3-ec-source] Thresholding one fixed smooth map separates the number of connected fields from the number of holes.
{{block:fig:PLACE-TOPOLOGY}}
A negative chi means that holes outnumber components in this 2D example. It does not mean a negative number of fields. When holes are absent, chi equals the component count. The expected Euler characteristic has an exact Gaussian formula even where identifying it with field count would be wrong. We already derived the 1D case. To understand the higher dimensional factors, we use a mathematical result: [for a smooth function on a compact domain whose [**critical point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s have zero gradient and invertible Hessians, the Euler characteristic of a level set region can be computed as a signed count of critical points, including boundary contributions. This is the relevant conclusion of [**Morse theory**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} We do not prove that topological theorem here. The calculation below shows how its Gaussian expectation produces the paper's polynomials and boundary terms; the general Gaussian result is given by Taylor's kinematic formula.[^p3-taylor] First take the interior of a $j$ dimensional region, with $j\le3$, and set $\lambda=\sigma^{-2}$. A critical point has gradient zero. The multidimensional Kac–Rice rule counts these zeros with the absolute Hessian determinant; the Morse signs replace that absolute determinant by $\det(-H)$. The resulting signed density above level $q$ is $$ \eta_j(q)=p_{\nabla z}(0) \int_q^\infty \mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid z=b,\nabla z=0]\,\phi(b)\,db, $$ where $\phi(b)=e^{-b^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$. The gradient's $j$ components are independent Gaussians of variance $\lambda$, so $p_{\nabla z}(0)=(2\pi\lambda)^{-j/2}$. The determinant measures how spatial volume near a gradient zero converts to gradient volume, just as the slope did for a scalar crossing. The resulting signed densities are $$ \eta_1=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma},\qquad \eta_2=\frac{q e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma^2},\qquad \eta_3=\frac{(q^2-1)e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^2\sigma^3}. $$ These are signed densities per length, area, and volume, not three formulas for positive field counts. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the Gaussian determinant average and its integrals"} Here are the Gaussian algebra steps behind the determinant average. Write the conditional Hessian as $H=-b\lambda I+G$, where $G$ has zero mean. Differentiating an isotropic covariance four times gives, for distinct indices $i,k$, $$ \mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}]=\kappa-\lambda^2, \qquad \mathbb E[G_{ik}^2]=\kappa. $$ The constant $\kappa$ describes a fourth derivative of covariance. Conditioning on height subtracts $\lambda^2$ from the covariance of the two diagonal entries, but not from the off-diagonal variance. Hence each pair contributes $$ \mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}-G_{ik}^2]=-\lambda^2. $$ For $j=1$, $\mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid b]=b\lambda$. For $j=2$, expand the two by two determinant to obtain $\lambda^2(b^2-1)$. For $j=3$, the leading term is $b^3\lambda^3$; the three index pairs each contribute $-b\lambda^3$, and all odd centered Gaussian products vanish. The result is $\lambda^3(b^3-3b)$. The unknown fourth derivative $\kappa$ has canceled. Integrating the three polynomials gives $$ \begin{aligned} \int_q^\infty b\phi(b)\,db&=\phi(q),\\ \int_q^\infty(b^2-1)\phi(b)\,db&=q\phi(q),\\ \int_q^\infty(b^3-3b)\phi(b)\,db&=(q^2-1)\phi(q). \end{aligned} $$ For example, differentiate $-q\phi(q)$ to get $(q^2-1)\phi(q)$, which verifies the second integral using its vanishing upper endpoint. Combining the determinant, gradient density, and integral gives the signed densities above. ::: Now include the boundary of an ordinary closed square or cube of side $L$, whose opposite faces are not joined and with every intersecting component retained. On a $j$ dimensional face, derivatives along the face give the same calculation as above. Each of its $d-j$ gradient components perpendicular to the face and directed out of the box must have the appropriate sign to contribute to the boundary Morse count. Symmetry and independence give a factor $2^{-(d-j)}$. There are $2^{d-j}\binom dj$ such faces, each of size $L^j$. Their combined coefficient is therefore $\binom djL^j$. Corners supply $Q(q)$ in total. With $r=L/\sigma$, the formulas become $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\chi_1]&=Q(q)+\frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_2]&=Q(q)+ \left[\frac{2r}{2\pi}+\frac{r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\right]e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_3]&=Q(q)+ \left[\frac{3r}{2\pi}+\frac{3r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} +\frac{r^3(q^2-1)}{(2\pi)^2}\right]e^{-q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These reproduce the paper's Equations 8–10 for interval, square, and cube geometry. They are not the formulas for a periodic box. For a rectangle or rectangular room, replace $2L$ or $3L$ by the sum of side lengths, $3L^2$ by the sum of pairwise side products, and $L^3$ by volume. A general domain requires its own geometric boundary factors. Applying only the volume term to a small room would discard real boundary contributions. The formulas have two limiting checks: - As $q\to-\infty$, the whole box becomes active and all three expectations tend to one. - As $q\to+\infty$, they tend to zero. At intermediate thresholds the higher dimensional signed densities can be negative because tunnels or holes outnumber components. For example a cube with $L/\sigma=10$ has expected $\chi=-20.06$ at $q=0$. A negative expected Euler characteristic is meaningful; a negative expected field count would not be. At a sufficiently high threshold, almost every component is a small solid blob with one peak and no holes. Then $\chi\simeq N$. For a large box, retaining the leading volume term and the leading power of $q$ gives $$ \mathbb E[N]\simeq \frac{V}{(2\pi)^{(d+1)/2}\sigma^d} q^{d-1}e^{-q^2/2}, $$ where $V$ is environment length, area, or volume. Dividing $VQ(q)$ by this count and using $Q(q)\simeq\phi(q)/q$ recovers $\mu_s\simeq(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/q)^d$, independently checking the size-law mean. [The exact EC formula and this approximate component count have different ranges of validity.]{.key-statement}[^p3-higher-count] Read Figure 3F–H as whole curves, rather than single field counts. Increasing the applied firing rate cutoff by $t\ge0$ changes the normalized level to $q+t/a$. It can reveal separation between peaks or remove components. The measured maps only test levels at or above their original effective cutoff; the rest of an analytic curve is a prediction. The gain was matched using mean maximum firing rate before the EC comparison, so the horizontal conversion from Hz to normalized level also uses fitted information. Two dimensional holes and three dimensional tunnels help explain the nonmonotonic curves.[^p3-ec-source] ## What was fitted and what was tested {#sec:PLACE-DATA} The experiments supply estimated firing rate maps, not the hidden Gaussian input. To assess a prediction, we must therefore track both which summaries set its parameters and which processing decisions change the map's geometry. The paper reanalyzes earlier bat and rodent recordings. It uses different available summaries in different conditions. The inspected article and supplement do not clearly give the final included cell count for every analysis, particularly the long-tunnel and 3D reanalyses; counts from an original recording study should therefore not be silently substituted for those final samples.[^p3-processing]
{{block:tbl:PLACE-DATA-COMPARISONS}}
The STAR Methods call the virtual-track animals rats in one sentence; Figure 1F and the main results identify them as mice. Several STAR figure cross-references also appear displaced. The table follows the main figure captions and the analyses described in full, rather than those isolated labels. Figure 1C distinguishes a limiting analytical Rayleigh curve from the finite threshold simulation histogram. Its parameters were constrained by both mean length and mean gap, so the full length histogram is an additional check. Figure 1D does the same for gaps. E tests skew and excess kurtosis of log lengths. For $Y=\log s$, write $m_k=\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb EY)^k]$; [then [**skew**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $m_3/m_2^{3/2}$ and [**excess kurtosis**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $m_4/m_2^2-3$. A [**lognormal distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} of sizes makes $Y$ Gaussian and both population quantities zero.]{.definition-explanation} Finite sample estimates still fluctuate, which is why the figure compares simulated sampling distributions.[^p3-fit-tests] For the long-tunnel data, the authors compared the Gaussian excursion model with a fitted lognormal using likelihoods and criteria that penalize fitted parameter count. Those comparisons favored the Gaussian model. [These are in-sample model comparisons. They are not reported held-out forecasts.]{.key-statement} Model histogram error bars come from $10^4$ simulations matched to the number of recorded cells; they do not quantify every source of animal-level or measurement uncertainty.[^p3-fit-tests] The processing choices affect the quantities being compared: - Bat maps were rectified at about 0.5 Hz for denoising. - The 3D maps, sampled in 10 cm bins, also received a median filter. - Fields larger than three standard deviations above mean 3D volume were removed as possible merges, including from slice analyses. - Peak counting excluded incomplete boundary fields and used a range of smoothing widths. - The 1D rate versus width comparison used an additional 1 Hz cutoff. [These decisions can remove small components, alter peaks, and change tails. They belong to the definition of the analyzed fields.]{.key-statement}[^p3-processing] The supplement adds useful checks. Figure S1 matches the rat maze's 15 cm minimum length cutoff in simulations and removes unusually large empirical fields; changing that cutoff changes log-length moments. Figure S5 shows sensitivity of the higher-moment comparison across small denoising thresholds, while the rate versus width slope becomes stable above about 1 Hz. Figure S2 compares the spherical-field alternative and measures boundary curvature. [Locally, [**mean curvature**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} averages bending in two principal directions and [**Gaussian curvature**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} multiplies them: a spherical patch bends the same way in both directions, while a saddle bends in opposite directions.]{.definition-explanation} These are extra shape measurements; they are not needed to derive the field-size law. Surface representations and finite differences affect their estimates.[^p3-supp-tests] Figure 4A–B summarizes fitted parameter changes across a small set of environments. The correlation length increases with environment size while the threshold generally decreases. Increasing $\sigma$ reduces crossings per metre; decreasing $q$ increases them. Both parameters also affect mean length, so these effects must be considered together. Figure S3 reports count scaling exponents below one and hence a weak decline in count per unit environment size. These cross-experiment trends do not establish a biological scaling law. In particular, the 3D table's reported $\sigma=4.0$ has an unclear distance-unit conversion relative to the spatial binning, so it should not be read as a verified value in metres.[^p3-trends] The model also allows differences between cells. Figure S4 draws a positive threshold separately for each cell and keeps that threshold for two otherwise independent maps representing opposite flight directions. Low-threshold cells tend to have more and larger fields in both maps; this shared cell property creates correlations between flight directions even when field locations differ between directions. Two distribution parameters were chosen to match the two empirical correlations, so those correlations are fitted features of this extension. Its continued agreement with length and gap distributions is the additional comparison. This extension should not be described as a two-parameter model shared by all cells.[^p3-threshold-variation] ## Random input weights can generate Gaussian maps {#sec:PLACE-WIRING} The statistical model becomes biologically useful if it suggests how a circuit could make the maps. A random weighted sum of many inputs is one possible mechanism, and the supplement makes its assumptions explicit. Let $u_i(x)$ be the fixed spatial tuning of input neuron $i$, and let independent weights $W_i$ have zero mean and variance $v_W$. The profiles $u_i$ may have nonzero spatial means. The expectation below is over weights: their zero means make the summed input $h(x)$ have mean zero. The summed input is $$ h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n W_i u_i(x). $$ [At a finite list of positions this is a sum of independent random vectors, one per input cell. Under a multivariate central limit condition, with a suitable normalization and no single input dominating, the sum approaches a Gaussian vector as the number of contributing inputs grows. Applying this at every finite list supplies the Gaussian-process description. The theorem needs many contributing inputs at the positions in question; a large anatomical input count alone does not show that this condition holds.]{.key-statement}[^p3-wiring-source] The covariance calculation exposes which assumption supplies spatial structure: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[h(x)h(y)] &=\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E[W_iW_j]u_i(x)u_j(y)\\ &=v_W\sum_i u_i(x)u_i(y). \end{aligned} $$ If inputs are translated copies $u_i(x)=u_0(x-x_i)$ with centres densely and uniformly covering space at density $\rho$, the sum is approximately $$ C(y-x)\simeq v_W\rho\int u_0(s)u_0(s+y-x)\,ds. $$ The assumptions supply different parts of the model: - Uniform coverage supplies stationarity away from boundaries. - Smooth input tuning supplies smoothness. - Random weights supply the Gaussian limit under their independence and size conditions. For input profiles with different shapes, average the last integral over the distribution of those shapes, as in Methods S2, Equation S8. For example, take $u_0(s)=R_0e^{-s^2/(2b^2)}$ in one dimension. # Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation {#ch:PLACE-TESTS} [Two maps can have the same field sizes and counts while arranging their active regions differently. One may contain rings or tunnels that the other lacks. Can the Gaussian spatial model account for these differences, and how much would that agreement tell us about the circuit that produced the maps?]{.key-statement} We first count connected regions and holes together, which gives a prediction across activity thresholds. The boundary of the observed environment matters for this calculation, so we keep its contributions. We then examine which measured quantities set the model's parameters and which provide further tests. Finally, a sum of many randomly weighted inputs shows one way a circuit could produce Gaussian spatial input, while making clear which assumptions and circuit measurements that explanation still needs. The map is still fixed over space. As before, $q$ is the normalized activity threshold, $\sigma$ is the local spatial scale, and $a$ converts normalized input above threshold into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is $d$; it is separate from the diffusion coefficient $D$ used in the memory chapters. ## Holes distinguish maps with the same field count {#sec:PLACE-TOPOLOGY} Two maps can have the same field count and total active area but different holes. As the activity threshold rises, active regions shrink and can split or disappear. The numbers of components and holes can change. [The [**Euler characteristic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, written $\chi$, combines these counts differently in each dimension:]{.definition-explanation} - In 1D it equals the number of connected active intervals. - In 2D it is the number of connected components minus the number of independent holes. Three disjoint disks have $\chi=3$; one connected ring has $\chi=1-1=0$. - In 3D it is components minus independent tunnels plus enclosed cavities. A solid ball has $\chi=1$, a solid ring has $\chi=0$, and a hollow spherical shell has $\chi=2$. [These counts are the first three [**Betti numbers**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: numbers of independent components, loops, and cavities, respectively.]{.definition-explanation}[^p3-ec-source] Thresholding one fixed smooth map separates the number of connected fields from the number of holes.
{{block:fig:PLACE-TOPOLOGY}}
A negative chi means that holes outnumber components in this 2D example. It does not mean a negative number of fields. When holes are absent, chi equals the component count. The expected Euler characteristic has an exact Gaussian formula even where identifying it with field count would be wrong. We already derived the 1D case. To understand the higher dimensional factors, we use a mathematical result: [for a smooth function on a compact domain whose [**critical point**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s have zero gradient and invertible Hessians, the Euler characteristic of a level set region can be computed as a signed count of critical points, including boundary contributions. This is the relevant conclusion of [**Morse theory**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} We do not prove that topological theorem here. The calculation below shows how its Gaussian expectation produces the paper's polynomials and boundary terms; the general Gaussian result is given by Taylor's kinematic formula.[^p3-taylor] First take the interior of a $j$ dimensional region, with $j\le3$, and set $\lambda=\sigma^{-2}$. A critical point has gradient zero. The multidimensional Kac–Rice rule counts these zeros with the absolute Hessian determinant; the Morse signs replace that absolute determinant by $\det(-H)$. The resulting signed density above level $q$ is $$ \eta_j(q)=p_{\nabla z}(0) \int_q^\infty \mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid z=b,\nabla z=0]\,\phi(b)\,db, $$ where $\phi(b)=e^{-b^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$. The gradient's $j$ components are independent Gaussians of variance $\lambda$, so $p_{\nabla z}(0)=(2\pi\lambda)^{-j/2}$. The determinant measures how spatial volume near a gradient zero converts to gradient volume, just as the slope did for a scalar crossing. The resulting signed densities are $$ \eta_1=\frac{e^{-q^2/2}}{2\pi\sigma},\qquad \eta_2=\frac{q e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\sigma^2},\qquad \eta_3=\frac{(q^2-1)e^{-q^2/2}}{(2\pi)^2\sigma^3}. $$ These are signed densities per length, area, and volume, not three formulas for positive field counts. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the Gaussian determinant average and its integrals"} Here are the Gaussian algebra steps behind the determinant average. Write the conditional Hessian as $H=-b\lambda I+G$, where $G$ has zero mean. Differentiating an isotropic covariance four times gives, for distinct indices $i,k$, $$ \mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}]=\kappa-\lambda^2, \qquad \mathbb E[G_{ik}^2]=\kappa. $$ The constant $\kappa$ describes a fourth derivative of covariance. Conditioning on height subtracts $\lambda^2$ from the covariance of the two diagonal entries, but not from the off-diagonal variance. Hence each pair contributes $$ \mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}-G_{ik}^2]=-\lambda^2. $$ For $j=1$, $\mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid b]=b\lambda$. For $j=2$, expand the two by two determinant to obtain $\lambda^2(b^2-1)$. For $j=3$, the leading term is $b^3\lambda^3$; the three index pairs each contribute $-b\lambda^3$, and all odd centered Gaussian products vanish. The result is $\lambda^3(b^3-3b)$. The unknown fourth derivative $\kappa$ has canceled. Integrating the three polynomials gives $$ \begin{aligned} \int_q^\infty b\phi(b)\,db&=\phi(q),\\ \int_q^\infty(b^2-1)\phi(b)\,db&=q\phi(q),\\ \int_q^\infty(b^3-3b)\phi(b)\,db&=(q^2-1)\phi(q). \end{aligned} $$ For example, differentiate $-q\phi(q)$ to get $(q^2-1)\phi(q)$, which verifies the second integral using its vanishing upper endpoint. Combining the determinant, gradient density, and integral gives the signed densities above. ::: Now include the boundary of an ordinary closed square or cube of side $L$, whose opposite faces are not joined and with every intersecting component retained. On a $j$ dimensional face, derivatives along the face give the same calculation as above. Each of its $d-j$ gradient components perpendicular to the face and directed out of the box must have the appropriate sign to contribute to the boundary Morse count. Symmetry and independence give a factor $2^{-(d-j)}$. There are $2^{d-j}\binom dj$ such faces, each of size $L^j$. Their combined coefficient is therefore $\binom djL^j$. Corners supply $Q(q)$ in total. With $r=L/\sigma$, the formulas become $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\chi_1]&=Q(q)+\frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_2]&=Q(q)+ \left[\frac{2r}{2\pi}+\frac{r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\right]e^{-q^2/2},\\ \mathbb E[\chi_3]&=Q(q)+ \left[\frac{3r}{2\pi}+\frac{3r^2q}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} +\frac{r^3(q^2-1)}{(2\pi)^2}\right]e^{-q^2/2}. \end{aligned} $$ These reproduce the paper's Equations 8–10 for interval, square, and cube geometry. They are not the formulas for a periodic box. For a rectangle or rectangular room, replace $2L$ or $3L$ by the sum of side lengths, $3L^2$ by the sum of pairwise side products, and $L^3$ by volume. A general domain requires its own geometric boundary factors. Applying only the volume term to a small room would discard real boundary contributions. The formulas have two limiting checks: - As $q\to-\infty$, the whole box becomes active and all three expectations tend to one. - As $q\to+\infty$, they tend to zero. At intermediate thresholds the higher dimensional signed densities can be negative because tunnels or holes outnumber components. For example a cube with $L/\sigma=10$ has expected $\chi=-20.06$ at $q=0$. A negative expected Euler characteristic is meaningful; a negative expected field count would not be. At a sufficiently high threshold, almost every component is a small solid blob with one peak and no holes. Then $\chi\simeq N$. For a large box, retaining the leading volume term and the leading power of $q$ gives $$ \mathbb E[N]\simeq \frac{V}{(2\pi)^{(d+1)/2}\sigma^d} q^{d-1}e^{-q^2/2}, $$ where $V$ is environment length, area, or volume. Dividing $VQ(q)$ by this count and using $Q(q)\simeq\phi(q)/q$ recovers $\mu_s\simeq(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/q)^d$, independently checking the size-law mean. [The exact EC formula and this approximate component count have different ranges of validity.]{.key-statement}[^p3-higher-count] Read Figure 3F–H as whole curves, rather than single field counts. Increasing the applied firing rate cutoff by $t\ge0$ changes the normalized level to $q+t/a$. It can reveal separation between peaks or remove components. The measured maps only test levels at or above their original effective cutoff; the rest of an analytic curve is a prediction. The gain was matched using mean maximum firing rate before the EC comparison, so the horizontal conversion from Hz to normalized level also uses fitted information. Two dimensional holes and three dimensional tunnels help explain the nonmonotonic curves.[^p3-ec-source] ## What was fitted and what was tested {#sec:PLACE-DATA} The experiments supply estimated firing rate maps, not the hidden Gaussian input. To assess a prediction, we must therefore track both which summaries set its parameters and which processing decisions change the map's geometry. The paper reanalyzes earlier bat and rodent recordings. It uses different available summaries in different conditions. The inspected article and supplement do not clearly give the final included cell count for every analysis, particularly the long-tunnel and 3D reanalyses; counts from an original recording study should therefore not be silently substituted for those final samples.[^p3-processing]
{{block:tbl:PLACE-DATA-COMPARISONS}}
The STAR Methods call the virtual-track animals rats in one sentence; Figure 1F and the main results identify them as mice. Several STAR figure cross-references also appear displaced. The table follows the main figure captions and the analyses described in full, rather than those isolated labels. Figure 1C distinguishes a limiting analytical Rayleigh curve from the finite threshold simulation histogram. Its parameters were constrained by both mean length and mean gap, so the full length histogram is an additional check. Figure 1D does the same for gaps. E tests skew and excess kurtosis of log lengths. For $Y=\log s$, write $m_k=\mathbb E[(Y-\mathbb EY)^k]$; [then [**skew**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $m_3/m_2^{3/2}$ and [**excess kurtosis**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is $m_4/m_2^2-3$. A [**lognormal distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} of sizes makes $Y$ Gaussian and both population quantities zero.]{.definition-explanation} Finite sample estimates still fluctuate, which is why the figure compares simulated sampling distributions.[^p3-fit-tests] For the long-tunnel data, the authors compared the Gaussian excursion model with a fitted lognormal using likelihoods and criteria that penalize fitted parameter count. Those comparisons favored the Gaussian model. [These are in-sample model comparisons. They are not reported held-out forecasts.]{.key-statement} Model histogram error bars come from $10^4$ simulations matched to the number of recorded cells; they do not quantify every source of animal-level or measurement uncertainty.[^p3-fit-tests] The processing choices affect the quantities being compared: - Bat maps were rectified at about 0.5 Hz for denoising. - The 3D maps, sampled in 10 cm bins, also received a median filter. - Fields larger than three standard deviations above mean 3D volume were removed as possible merges, including from slice analyses. - Peak counting excluded incomplete boundary fields and used a range of smoothing widths. - The 1D rate versus width comparison used an additional 1 Hz cutoff. [These decisions can remove small components, alter peaks, and change tails. They belong to the definition of the analyzed fields.]{.key-statement}[^p3-processing] The supplement adds useful checks. Figure S1 matches the rat maze's 15 cm minimum length cutoff in simulations and removes unusually large empirical fields; changing that cutoff changes log-length moments. Figure S5 shows sensitivity of the higher-moment comparison across small denoising thresholds, while the rate versus width slope becomes stable above about 1 Hz. Figure S2 compares the spherical-field alternative and measures boundary curvature. [Locally, [**mean curvature**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} averages bending in two principal directions and [**Gaussian curvature**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} multiplies them: a spherical patch bends the same way in both directions, while a saddle bends in opposite directions.]{.definition-explanation} These are extra shape measurements; they are not needed to derive the field-size law. Surface representations and finite differences affect their estimates.[^p3-supp-tests]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S1}}
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S5
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S5}}
Figure 4A–B summarizes fitted parameter changes across a small set of environments. The correlation length increases with environment size while the threshold generally decreases. Increasing $\sigma$ reduces crossings per metre; decreasing $q$ increases them. Both parameters also affect mean length, so these effects must be considered together. Figure S3 reports count scaling exponents below one and hence a weak decline in count per unit environment size. These cross-experiment trends do not establish a biological scaling law. In particular, the 3D table's reported $\sigma=4.0$ has an unclear distance-unit conversion relative to the spatial binning, so it should not be read as a verified value in metres.[^p3-trends]
Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure 4

Original paper figure: Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025), Figure S3
{{block:fig:PAPER-PLACE-S3}}
The model also allows differences between cells. Figure S4 draws a positive threshold separately for each cell and keeps that threshold for two otherwise independent maps representing opposite flight directions. Low-threshold cells tend to have more and larger fields in both maps; this shared cell property creates correlations between flight directions even when field locations differ between directions. Two distribution parameters were chosen to match the two empirical correlations, so those correlations are fitted features of this extension. Its continued agreement with length and gap distributions is the additional comparison. This extension should not be described as a two-parameter model shared by all cells.[^p3-threshold-variation]

# Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor {#ch:MEMORY-DYNAMICS} [A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value that the stimulus supplied.]{.key-statement} The important question is whether the activity pattern stays in the right place, not just whether activity continues. Burak and Fiete study this distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set.[^p1-model] To calculate the loss of accuracy, we first describe how spikes renew synaptic activity as it decays. We then follow a small disturbance through the circuit's return toward a stable pattern and identify the change in stored value that remains. Adding these lasting random changes gives a local rate of spreading. When connections have equal weights in both directions, we can express that rate using the cells' tuning curves and check its meaning in a two-cell example. The following chapter asks how this local prediction extends to longer delays. Paper and Supporting Information (SI) links open the cited PDF page, near the passage where the viewer supports it. Use the equation, figure, or paragraph label to find the passage; the PDFs have no numbered text lines. The memory coordinate is $\theta$. Its initial value is $\Theta$. A bar denotes a noise free steady state, so $\bar r_i(\theta)$ is neuron $i$'s steady firing rate at memory value $\theta$. The common synaptic time constant is $\tau$. A one dimensional diffusion coefficient $D$ has units of memory coordinate squared per time, with the convention $\operatorname{Var}[\theta(t)-\Theta]=2Dt$ when $D$ is constant and boundaries do not matter. ## Recurrent spikes renew decaying synaptic activity {#sec:MEMORY-SPIKES} **Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. [Incoming activations determine new firing rates; the resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.]{.key-statement} The model assumes fixed connection weights, constant biases, a common synaptic decay time, and independent Poisson spike counts conditional on the present rates. The connections are tuned to a continuous family of steady patterns. The Gaussian description below also assumes weak fluctuations in total input. **Mathematical derivation.** To combine discrete events with continuous decay, a count process records the events and a decay equation records how their effects fade. Here $N_i(t)$ counts neuron $i$'s spikes up to time $t$. The activation $s_i$ tracks the decaying synaptic effect of those outgoing spikes on receiving cells. S14–S15, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=3&zoom=125,0,576)) $$ \boxed{2D(\theta)=\sum_i v_i(\theta)^2\bar r_i(\theta).} $$ For several memory coordinates $\theta_\alpha$, choose tangent vectors $u_i^\alpha=\partial\bar s_i/\partial\theta_\alpha$ and left vectors with $\sum_i v_i^\alpha u_i^\beta=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$. The same covariance calculation gives $$ 2D_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i v_i^\alpha\bar r_i v_i^\beta. $$ **Interpretation.** For one memory coordinate, each neuron's contribution combines its spike variability, $\bar r_i$, with the squared effect of one activation fluctuation on the final memory, $v_i^2$. The formula does not say that neurons with high rates necessarily damage memory more: changing rates can also change the tuning curves and the projection weights. Those changes must be included in a comparison.[^p1-projection] The result is local in state and leading order in weak noise. The time interval must satisfy two conditions: - It must be long enough for the approximation based on many spike contributions to apply. - It must be short enough that the coefficients do not change substantially as the memory moves. These conditions justify a local spreading rate. Systematic drift requires a [separate check in the next chapter](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-drift-scope). [The [**diffusion tensor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the matrix of displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time.]{.definition-explanation} Its diagonal entries describe spreading in individual coordinates; its other entries describe how coordinate displacements vary together. Even independently generated spike-count fluctuations can generate coupled motion of the represented coordinates.[^p1-multid] ## Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves {#sec:MEMORY-SYMMETRIC} **Neural mechanism.** The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. [When $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$, can we express it through the tuning curves and neural transfer function?]{.key-statement} Symmetric connections make each cell affect another cell's input with the same weight that it receives in return, while their firing responses can still differ. We retain the common synaptic time constant, a stable continuous family, and the weak noise and conditional independence assumptions. **Mathematical derivation.** The chain rule relates the slope of a response curve to the slope of its input curve. Here let $g_i'=d\bar g_i/d\theta$ and $r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$. Differentiating the fixed point identities gives $$ r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i', \qquad \mathbf g'=\tau W\mathbf r'. $$ With symmetric $W$, the transpose of the linearized matrix satisfies $$ K^T\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\operatorname{diag}[\phi'(\bar g_i)]\mathbf g' =-\mathbf g'/\tau+W\mathbf r'=0. $$ Therefore $\mathbf v$ is proportional to $\mathbf g'$. Its normalization is $$ v_i=\frac{g_i'}{\tau\sum_jr_j'g_j'}, $$ because $u_i=\tau r_i'$. Substituting into the noise projection gives $$ \boxed{ 2D(\theta)= \frac{\sum_i\bar r_i(g_i')^2} {\tau^2[\sum_i r_i'g_i']^2}. } $$ **Interpretation.** The input slopes $g_i'$ now determine the projection weights, so the diffusion coefficient can be calculated from the tuning curves and transfer function. This follows from [SI Eq. S18, p. 4](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,239), with $\bar g_i=\phi^{-1}(\bar r_i)$ wherever the transfer function is invertible over the relevant range. The supplied Early Edition [main Eq. 2, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,88) appears to omit the square on $g_i'$ in the numerator; the projection calculation and SI S18 give the squared expression shown here. This is an independent source check, not an author-confirmed correction. The result requires: - symmetric weights; - a stable continuous family; - the noise assumptions already introduced. The result does not require translation symmetry, in which shifting an activity pattern along the represented coordinate leaves the network dynamics unchanged in form.[^p1-symmetric]
**Example: opposite firing changes with constant diffusion.** Take two mutually inhibiting cells with $W_{12}=W_{21}=-1$, zero self weights, equal biases $b$, and $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ over the positive input range. Its fixed points obey $$ \bar s_1=\frac{b+\theta}{2},\qquad \bar s_2=\frac{b-\theta}{2},\qquad |\theta| {{block:fig:MEMORY-INHIBITION-RATES}}

# Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays {#ch:MEMORY-LONG-DELAYS} [A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait.]{.key-statement} The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone. We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows. Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift. ## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} **Neural mechanism.** Spike fluctuations keep shifting the stored value after the cue has ended. The local diffusion coefficient describes the variance of those shifts after stable disturbances have relaxed. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever: boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. We first keep $D$ constant, so the line and circle differ only in how the memory coordinate is bounded. **Mathematical derivation.** Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. [The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.]{.definition-explanation} A density equation tracks how small random increments redistribute probability. The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$; constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the upper density approaches uniform, the wrapped error below approaches $\pi^2/3$; the line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a curved variance versus time graph. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=10&zoom=125,0,45). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}
## A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift {#sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE} **Neural mechanism.** [Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question. [The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] **Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network. With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. **Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift; they cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average.]{.key-statement} A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions. The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. Calculating the corresponding Fisher information would require the matching joint likelihood. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)); it does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation] ## Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-FIGURES} **Neural mechanism in the figures.** [Figure 1A, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,439) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization). [In Fig. 1B, an [**activity bump**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a localized peak of population firing rates across the neurons' preferred angles.]{.definition-explanation} The figure separates two sources of error: - During storage, the bump's location has moved away from its initial value $\Theta$. - At the later time, an observer has additional uncertainty about the bump's current location because it sees only a finite sample of spikes. The [information calculation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures this second uncertainty and relates it to diffusion; the [readout chapter](ch-memory-readout.html) then follows observation of the moving state.[^p1-fig1]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-1}}
[Figure 2, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3&zoom=125,0,18) tests the diffusion calculation in two different network designs. Panel A shows a ring with weights determined by differences of preferred angles. This gives rotational symmetry: rotating the activity pattern around the ring leaves its dynamics unchanged in form. In B, compare the firing rate curves and spike marks in the inset before reading the wandering angular trace. The curve describes rates; the marks are particular random spike events. The trace shows the represented angle rather than overall activity amplitude. **Interpretation of the simulation tests.** Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction: - Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. - Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals; its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$. Panels E to G use mutual inhibition rather than a ring. The two rates in F vary in opposite directions; their difference represents memory. Panel G compares their displacement statistics with the analytic prediction. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-2}}
The derivation has now supplied a dynamical quantity, $D$, from spike variability and the way a network returns to its attractor. We next derive a statistical quantity from the same tuning curves and ask why it puts a lower limit on $D$. [^p1-fp]: Burak, Y., & Fiete, I. R. (2012). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*, Supporting Text: [density equation, Eqs. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483); [angular error, Eq. S32, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,48). S38–S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,48); [Fig. S1, p. 10](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=10&zoom=125,0,45). The calculation below first obtains that equation for a general state-dependent $D$; constant $D$ then gives the line and circle solutions. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the density equation below. ::: [In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:]{.definition-explanation} $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ [Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ **Interpretation.** [The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.]{.key-statement}[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the upper density approaches uniform, the wrapped error below approaches $\pi^2/3$; the line error keeps growing. **Neural mechanism.** The rate of random spreading can change as the stored value changes, because the current firing rates set the spike variability. The supplement illustrates this dependence with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. **Mathematical derivation.** When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602).[^p1-variable] For the mutual excitation network, substituting $v_1=v_2=1/2$ into the diffusion formula gives $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ **Interpretation.** A state dependent $D$ need not produce a curved variance versus time graph. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain. The implied variance for this network is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-s1). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure S1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-S1}}
## A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift {#sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE} **Neural mechanism.** [Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.]{.key-statement} Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question. [The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor.]{.definition-explanation} A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] **Mathematical derivation.** For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. [The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments.]{.definition-explanation} With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network. With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. **Interpretation.** The variance calculation captures the leading random term. [Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift; they cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average.]{.key-statement} A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions. The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. Calculating the corresponding Fisher information would require the matching joint likelihood. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)); it does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation] ## Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-FIGURES} **Neural mechanism in the figures.** [Figure 1A, p. 2](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-1) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization). [In Fig. 1B, an [**activity bump**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a localized peak of population firing rates across the neurons' preferred angles.]{.definition-explanation} The figure separates two sources of error: - During storage, the bump's location has moved away from its initial value $\Theta$. - At the later time, an observer has additional uncertainty about the bump's current location because it sees only a finite sample of spikes. The [information calculation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures this second uncertainty and relates it to diffusion; the [readout chapter](ch-memory-readout.html) then follows observation of the moving state.[^p1-fig1]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-MEMORY-1}}
[Figure 2, p. 3](ch-memory-long-delays.html#fig-paper-memory-2) tests the diffusion calculation in two different network designs. Panel A shows a ring with weights determined by differences of preferred angles. This gives rotational symmetry: rotating the activity pattern around the ring leaves its dynamics unchanged in form. In B, compare the firing rate curves and spike marks in the inset before reading the wandering angular trace. The curve describes rates; the marks are particular random spike events. The trace shows the represented angle rather than overall activity amplitude. **Interpretation of the simulation tests.** Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction: - Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. - Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals; its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$. Panels E to G use mutual inhibition rather than a ring. The two rates in F vary in opposite directions; their difference represents memory. Panel G compares their displacement statistics with the analytic prediction. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2]
Original paper figure: Burak and Fiete (2012), Figure 2
